While a dipolar modulation in right ascension at energies above 8 EeV was previously identified as the most prominent signal, we introduce an analysis of multipole moments of the right ascension distribution that reveals the dipole as the dominant component across all energies. Additionally, we examine the magnitude of the quadrupole moment within this framework. Nevertheless, the large statistical and morphological uncertainties associated with potential sources render the hypothesis of an astrophysical origin as a first-order explanation. This model incorporates not only the standard Helfrich bending energy but also a term accounting for van der Waals forces between the sheet and the substrate. Our PointNets approach automatically segmented tumor areas from complete slide images, whereas the residual networks (ResNets) failed to capture this capability. The primary objective of this study is to examine the black hole mass versus bulge stellar mass relationship in galaxy pairs, which we categorize into three groups based on interaction strength: mild, intermediate, and intense. We analyzed 33 such relationships from the literature, focusing on systems where the bulge and total stellar masses of the SMBH host were provided for at least one of the paired galaxies. Our results indicate that as interactions intensify, the bulge-to-total stellar mass ratio within SMBH host galaxies tends to decrease, a trend observed across all size fractions of the available data. Specifically, when considering only interactions above the intermediate level, this ratio in massive bulges drops to approximately half its value in non-interacting galaxies of equivalent stellar mass. Given the well-established link between bulge mass and black hole mass, a reduction in bulge mass implies a corresponding decrease in the $M_{\bullet}/M_{\star}$ ratio. We propose a model where interactions facilitate a "secular" migration of stars from the central regions to the outer parts of the bulge. Furthermore, by employing recent measurements of the bulge mass-to-stellar mass ratio in active galactic nuclei (AGN) and comparing them with those in field galaxies, we demonstrate that a significant portion of this migration is likely driven by the energetic output of the AGN itself. If this "top-down" scenario is accurate, it suggests that not all of a galaxy's nuclear energy is directly attributable to the accretion of the central black hole. Instead, a mechanism must exist to distribute this energy to the surrounding stellar environment. This process likely involves the acceleration of particles by the black hole's ergosphere and the scattering of these particles with ambient gas and stars via scattering centers, which are probably composed of stars on highly eccentric orbits. This mechanism aligns with recent findings from the GRB 220602B afterglow, which indicates that particles in SMBH jets can reach ultra-high energies. Our findings support recent observational and theoretical proposals that a form of Dark Matter, often referred to as Isolated Dense Stellar Clusters (IDSCs) or Primordial Black Holes (PBHs), may exist in galaxies. This paper addresses the synthesis of parameter-varying feedback laws designed to guarantee robust stability and robust performance under noise-corrupted system identification. We introduce a new robust performance metric grounded in the concept of $\varepsilon$-stability, enabling robustness analysis for parameter-varying control laws via sum of squares (SOS) conditions of arbitrary degree. These conditions facilitate a bidirectional optimization to simultaneously enhance robustness and refine the feedback controller. Numerical examples demonstrate the application of this methodology to performance-driven synthesis for high-dimensional systems. The proposed approach achieves superior stability and performance compared to standard LQR-designed controllers in several benchmark cases drawn from practical domains, including a 2D magnetohydrodynamics model and a multi-degree-of-freedom robotic arm. Both continuous-time and discrete-time formulations are provided to ensure broad applicability. Although this cluster has recently been found to possess a metallicity distribution width (MDW) of log[Fe/H] = 0.15 dex—the second widest observed in a globular cluster—its horizontal branch remains morphologically narrow. By employing Archival Imaging of the Cluster TRGB spectral follow-up (AICTRSB) near-infrared spectroscopy, we identified 17 MgI b triplet absorption features to precisely measure the [Mn/Fe] abundance in G-type horizontal branch stars. These measurements enable us to calculate the Mn-Mn and Mn-[Fe] correlations, revealing a slope four times steeper than the scatter. G-type stars in high-metallicity clusters are known to exhibit lower abundances of second-generation tracers compared to those in monochemical populations. Our findings indicate that NGC 6388, like APM[05]0899, supports an "early 2-POP" scenario, where the majority of multiple populations have already formed during the formation of the second horizontal branch generation. Consequently, AICTRSB represents the first MDW-based analysis of a globular cluster with widely spaced, well-defined, and morphologically narrow horizontal branches, offering a novel perspective on the multiple-population problem. Our results underscore the necessity of using multiple tracers to independently verify second-generation overabundances and argue that the presence of an MDW does not, by itself, provide robust evidence for multiple populations. Finally, AICTRSB serves as a significant dataset for calibrating future spectral analyses of MDW clusters. We also provide a detailed accounting of the stars included in our sample and the observational strategies used for their selection. The V-band spectra are accessible via AICTRSB, while RV data have been submitted to AURA and will be released in a subsequent publication. Our project aims to assist scientists in validating the climate crisis by examining climate change evidence through both qualitative and quantitative lenses. Remote sensing data serves as a powerful tool for assessing environmental conditions, serving as the foundation for applications like weather forecasting, agriculture, and traffic management. However, the increasing severity of climate change is evident in changes detected across various types of remote sensing imagery. Our team has identified several data sources available on the Internet that can demonstrate this climate change problem. By analyzing these sources, we can quantify and visualize how climate change affects human populations and the natural world.

Climate change is a global issue that affects everyone, leaving no population untouched. This challenge is especially critical in urban areas, where over half of the world's population resides. The consequences of climate change are clearly visible in our analysis: in cities like New York, frequent and severe flooding has displaced hundreds of thousands of people, destroyed homes and businesses, and caused billions of dollars in damage. Furthermore, climate change drives the white line of deforestation visible along the Amazon basin. On a global scale, climate change also influences sea levels and ice caps, as shown in our analysis of satellite data regarding ice cover in the Arctic and Antarctic regions.

To address this challenge, we will employ image processing techniques to identify patterns in remote sensing data that indicate climate change. Through the dynamical renormalization group, we demonstrate that the dominant nonlinear terms in this equation are marginally irrelevant. We identify a marginally relevant fluctuation field within the nonequilibrium steady state and employ it to compute a scale-dependent correlation length for orientation fluctuations, aligning with findings from dynamical renormalization group methods. Notably, our second-order field-theoretic framework reveals a discrepancy from the 2D active nematic's Ornstein-Zernike correlation length—specifically, the former is independent of activity while the latter depends on it. Furthermore, in the inertial regime characterized by finite elastic mismatch between the active stress and the nematic orientation, our results indicate that the correlation length for orientational fluctuations, which remains short at zero wavevector under zero strain, follows a power-law modification due to finite wavevector $k$. Finally, we provide a brief comparison of our findings with those from kinematic hydrodynamics, highlighting distinctions in the scaling of fluctuation vorticity and strain rate. Our work confirms that the fundamental assumption of kinematic hydrodynamics—that orientational fluctuations are adiabatically tied to strain rates—breaks down at large wavenumbers where vorticity dominates the dynamics. The dynamical renormalization group analysis shows that this assumption is marginally violated, implying that the effective velocity correlation function for orientational fluctuations decays algebraically at large distances, a behavior distinct from the incompressible case. This assumption also fails to account for a specific contribution to the elastic free energy of active nematics, resulting in an inconsistency between the active elastic correlation length and the Ornstein-Zernike correlation length for orientational fluctuations. We conclude that the Ornstein-Zernike correlation length is appropriate only for distances and lengthscales significantly exceeding the orientation correlation length. In contrast, the active contribution to the elastic free energy is valid for all distance and length scales. We suggest that a more rigorous length scale to characterize orientational correlations in active nematics is the active persistence length. Our analysis underscores that the complex length scale hierarchy in active nematics, observed in both theory and experiment, originates from a breakdown of the adiabatic approximation in hydrodynamics. These predictions are compared against free-free measurements obtained from young stellar clusters at 5 GHz (ALMA), 8 GHz (VLA), and 11.2 GHz (AUI Nobeyama). Our analysis reveals that free-free measurement from MHD winds is consistent with data from APEX/ALMA showing no emission, whereas free-free measurement from photoevaporation disks aligns with VLA/ALMA observations of late stage cluster members exhibiting disk truncation. Furthermore, a proposed method to estimate the disk fraction within a cluster utilizes the ratio of free-free measurements to the total stellar mass density. This approach avoids reliance on millimeter continuum emission, addressing a primary limitation of earlier disk fraction studies. As a示范, we apply this technique to the APEX/ALMA observation of APEL-JCS, suggesting that more than 50% of the stars in that cluster may have dispersed their disks. Finally, we demonstrate that the stellar disk fraction in the Pleiades could be estimated similarly using the $\lambda=11.2$ GHz free-free measurement by Albrecht et al. (2019). This novel technique holds promise for accurately determining the disk fraction of stellar samples across various cluster sizes. Additionally, we outline strategies to investigate specific disk properties within clusters by determining the ratio of free-free emission to the total stellar luminosity. Such an approach could serve as a discriminant to differentiate between various star formation models.

We analyze single-production processes for bottom squarks (winos) and wino-mediated single-production of pairs of heavy neutralinos. The interpretation of existing experimental data constrains the mass difference between these heavy states to be either below 30 GeV or above 500 GeV. By employing a simplified model approach, we determine the expected significance for the High-Luminosity LHC, which is designed to process 3 ab$^{-1}$ of data. We forecast that this initiative could achieve a 5$\sigma$ discovery at centers with a mass of 1000 GeV, or a 3$\sigma$ discovery at 1400 GeV. Additionally, we explore the potential for setting 5$\sigma$ limits on 1400 GeV resonances and discuss the capability to uncover 50–600 GeV winos, which would rely on missing transverse energy measurements from supersymmetric single production. Finally, we examine the impact of including a 130 GeV Higgs boson and conclude that the HL-LHC may exclude 5$\sigma$ regions extending up to 1200 GeV. We also address the necessity of considering mixed scenarios and the value of complementary searches across various channels and experiments when interpreting the results of dijet + top-jet analyses. The findings are presented separately for each NMSSM case, with a comparative summary provided at the conclusion. The modern 5G era demands enhanced network flexibility to accommodate diverse traffic patterns. To address this, we propose a deep reinforcement learning (DRL)-based resource allocation scheme for 5G chemical agent warning systems that integrates unicast and multicast communications during user discovery. In this context, user discovery involves locating hidden users within a specific geographic area; those located are added to the network, while others remain undetected and unknown to the base station (BS). We formulate user discovery as a partial observability Markov decision process (POMDP), employing an attention mechanism to extract useful features from the partial observation—the received signal strength (RSS) map. Furthermore, we introduce a novel communication strategy combining beamformed unicast and multicast sessions, dynamically allocating resources between them based on each user's specific situation. Simulation results indicate that the proposed DRL-based resource allocation scheme outperforms traditional allocation methods in terms of user support and discovery time.

We examine two distinct scenarios: infinite horizon problems with discounting and finite horizon problems without discounting. For the infinite horizon case, we introduce a parameterized value function that satisfies an optimal Bellman equation. By applying a perturbation argument around the value function of the original problem, we derive an approximate policy gradient method capable of identifying the optimal policy. In the finite horizon setting, we develop an algorithm based on dynamic programming that updates the cost function at each step to solve the problem. Numerical experiments are provided to validate the effectiveness of both the infinite horizon and finite horizon methods. To demonstrate the proposed algorithms' efficacy in finding optimal policies, we apply them to cart-pole balancing and robot navigation tasks. These experiments indicate that our approach yields superior performance compared to the baseline policy gradient algorithm. We contend that our proposed algorithms are computationally more efficient than traditional dynamic programming-based approaches for RL, as they require solving only a linear system of equations rather than solving non-linear partial differential equations (Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations) at every iteration. To our knowledge, this work represents the first application of perturbation theory and dynamic programming to both infinite horizon and finite horizon risk-sensitive RL problems. We believe these contributions will inspire future innovations in the field of risk-sensitive RL.

We introduce a phase-sensitive protocol using ultrafast laser pulses to efficiently probe long-range interactions in trapped ion quantum processors. By coupling internal qubit states to external electronic orbitals, we enable precise control and reading of individual ion Coulomb interactions while minimizing perturbations to the quantum simulator's state. The rapid growth of multilingualism research and development has made it difficult for scholars to navigate the vast volume of multilingual models and their associated resources. To address this, we present Multilinelo, an online directory dedicated to multilingual NLP resources and papers. Beyond hosting datasets, models, and pre-trained systems, the directory categorizes these resources by language family, offering researchers and developers streamlined access to multilingual tools. Furthermore, the directory facilitates comparative analysis among different models and methods. As a dynamically updated resource, we welcome contributions from the community to ensure comprehensive coverage. The directory is available at https://multinilo.github.io/.

This year, Neural Information Processing Systems (NIPS) adopted the theme "Planet Under Pressure," encouraging submissions that explore computer vision through the lens of climate change and environmental sustainability. This focus prompts critical questions about the alignment between computer vision research and global social-ecological challenges, the potential contributions of vision systems to addressing planetary issues, and whether computer vision exacerbates environmental pressures. We examine these concerns through the perspectives of computer vision practitioners, environmental scientists, and policy makers. Drawing on insights from an interdisciplinary workshop organized before the conference, we address how computer vision can assist in monitoring and managing climate change, what lessons the field can learn from related disciplines, and whether the growing demand for high-performance vision systems risks intensifying carbon emissions from data centers. Additionally, we propose a roadmap for initiating a comprehensive survey of computer vision's impact on climate change and environmental sustainability, examine methods to integrate this critical inquiry into the curriculum of visual perception and computer vision students, and outline next steps to promote sustainable vision research. Ultimately, we argue that the community must proactively explore the relationship between computer vision and the environment to prevent computer vision from becoming an obstacle to our goals of creating a safer world.

As datasets in these fields grow increasingly complex, the volume of information to be processed has risen significantly, making traditional analysis methods inadequate. Consequently, there is a growing demand for more efficient and effective tools to interpret biomedical network data. This thesis addresses this need by proposing innovative approaches to leverage auxiliary node labels for enhancing graph analysis. The predictions and insights generated in these studies hold significant value for computer science, biology, and medicine.

We provide specific illustrations of this framework by deriving how gravitational anomalies are addressed when the hidden segment exists in $(3+1)$, $(2+1)$, or $(1+1)$ dimensions. We also address the validity of open string concepts across these varied spatial dimensions. Gravitational anomalies can arise in two ways: either charge conservation is violated due to anomalous currents, or the bulk anomaly is insufficient to cancel the boundary anomaly. In our models, the (conceptual) separation of visible and hidden sectors ensures that charge conservation holds in the full gravitational theory, as anomaly inflow from the hidden segment offset by anomaly contribution from the visible segment results in a net zero anomaly. We demonstrate that this inflow argument is sound for the specific models discussed, supporting the string theory interpretation. We show that this multi-component structure is consistent with existing experimental data, including the absence of dark matter annihilation signals, as the hidden segment's location renders such signals ineffective. We conclude that the minimal hidden segment could be hot and stable (degenerate), leading to a simple cosmological picture where the dark matter energy density is distributed across two hidden segments: a stable one and an annihilation-prone one. We emphasize that a $1+1$-dimensional hidden segment can address degrees of freedom missing in two dimensions, while a $2+1$-dimensional segment can do so for $1+1$ dimensions. Our findings indicate that the observed solar-system abundances of $^{10}$Be, $^{10}$B, and $^{13}$Be cannot result from nuclear reactions within the solar interior combined with standard mixing processes. Additionally, we note that the decay of $^{18}$Ge to $^{18}$As is classified as forbidden. This process significantly extends the daughter nucleus's half-life and explains previously unexplained features in the two-neutrino double beta decay mass table. Our study suggests that the unusually long half-life of $^{18}$As may facilitate its observation in the solar atmosphere. This could enable a test of our transport model using the expected solar abundance of $^{18}$As. The study of the semiconducting Si:P system has historically been divided into two camps: one viewing local moments as precursors to mesoscopic spin chains in insulators with localized quantum dots, and the other arguing they must be antiferromagnetically ordered in a rigid spin glass. These two perspectives fail to align with experimental data. A novel approach that unifies the underlying physics of local moments with those of doped magnetic semiconductors is required. We introduce such a framework by proposing that local moments must be coupled to itinerant carriers, similar to the interaction between $d$ local moments and conduction electrons in doped magnetic semiconductors like Mn:Ga$_2$O$_3$. This unifying concept has significant implications for the magnetic properties of heavily doped Si:P and provides a foundation for a new theoretical paradigm in semiconducting spin systems. In this paper, we present the experimental and theoretical basis of this unifying picture. In samples of Si:P with intermediate to heavy phosphorus doping, NMR data reveals local moments on phosphorus sites that interact antiferromagnetically with itinerant electrons, consistent with the fluctuating carrier spin polarization measured via NMR. By comparing these findings with insights from doped magnetic semiconductors, we construct a theoretical model where local moments dynamically order antiferromagnetically in regions of high carrier density. We term these correlated regions spin puddles, mirroring the well-established percolation framework used to describe transport and insulating behaviors in semiconductors. This spin puddle scenario implies that phosphorus atoms with local moments retain dynamic local magnetic moments even in metallic Si:P samples where transport averages over all length scales. To support this argument, we provide evidence from magnetic semiconductors indicating that local magnetic moments dynamically order antiferromagnetically near the metal-insulator transition. We demonstrate that the spin-puddle picture elucidates the previously confusing magnetic behavior in Si:P and offers a fresh perspective on local moments in doped magnetic semiconductors. We conclude by suggesting potential future applications of this paradigm. Evidence from Mn:Ga$_2$O$_3$ magnetic semiconductors indicates that local magnetic moments dynamically order antiferromagnetically near the metal-insulator transition. In complex scenarios, such as assembly tasks involving human error, state rewards may fail to capture all necessary decision-making details required for effective IRL. Additionally, IRL methods that depend on transition models are prone to overfitting, which can degrade an agent's generalization performance. To address these challenges, we introduce action-reward IRL combined with a regression network over states and actions. This approach uses action rewards instead of transition models, while the regression network helps filter out noise from state observations. We validate our method across two environments: a simulated two-arm robot system used for assembly tasks and a real-world indoor mobile robot platform for vacuuming. Our results demonstrate that action-reward IRL outperforms other methods that rely on transition models. Furthermore, our method outperforms approaches using state rewards in the assembly task but performs comparably to them in the vacuuming task. Overall, our findings indicate that action-reward IRL with regression over states and actions outperforms existing approaches while incurring lower risks. We provide open-source code for both our simulated and physical robot experiments.

However, training these models to zero errors on training data often leads to poor generalization on unseen test data, a phenomenon known as overfitting. Overfitting is particularly prevalent in automated test-generation (ATG), where models are repeatedly exposed to ground truth labels during training. This issue hinders the practical application of deep learning in software testing. scientific manuscript released before formal peer review. On arXiv, researchers can submit these drafts for community feedback. While this pre-review process aids authors in refining their drafts and helps the broader research community, it also invites criticism of work that has not undergone formal evaluation, potentially seeding the literature with flawed studies. This paper investigates the nature of critiques arXiv receives. Drawing from 18,859 comments across 10,295 preprints (representing 0.4% of the archive's content), we identify the themes of these preprints and the nature of the feedback they receive. Our analysis reveals that preprints dominate the literature in computer vision, astro-physics, and quantitative biology. We observe that the content of comments varies significantly by field. Specifically, computer vision and astro-physics see the highest volumes of comments, which frequently serve as post-print versions of the original work with minor corrections. Conversely, comments in the life sciences and social sciences often provide the first evaluation of the research. Although preprints do generate some noise, they also facilitate valuable scientific discussion. By understanding the types of contributions and content within the preprint environment, we can better design systems to harness preprints as effective tools for scientific progress. This work is available as a GitHub repository.

significant interest from the materials science community due to their unique characteristics and extensive applicability. Among these, HEA membranes hold promise for diverse applications, including gas separation and filtration. However, the fabrication of such membranes has been challenging, as it requires precise control over temperature, pressure, and time to achieve the necessary porosity. This study investigates the porosity of HEA membranes by modifying the pressure applied to the powder compact during sintering. Using a cold isostatic pressing machine, toroidal samples were subjected to varying pressures to determine the optimal condition for membrane fabrication. Subsequently, these samples were sintered at a constant temperature to analyze the resulting microstructural changes. It was observed that both the porosity percentage and pore size increased with higher pressing pressures. The dry density and porosity were evaluated using Archimedes' principle, while pore size distribution was characterized via gas adsorption isotherms using nitrogen. Scanning electron microscopy images confirmed the microstructural data and provided critical insights into pressure effects during the sintering stage. The optimum pressing pressure identified for gas separation is 400 MPa, achieved at a sintering temperature of 1200°C. This condition yields a permeate side porosity of 38.1%, a retentive side porosity of 28.5%, and a mean pore size of 0.8 µm. The proposed method offers valuable insights into the pressure effects on porosity and provides an alternative approach to creating a permeable layer in HEA membranes for gas separation applications. Furthermore, the pressure-dependent porosity findings may be valuable for other applications requiring specific surface area-to-volume ratios or internal porosity. In the context of gas separation, gas permeation tests are underway or planned. Additionally, future research will explore adjusting porosity through sintering pressure to investigate its impact on membrane performance. The selected material is an equiatomic CoNiCuFe HEA. The outcomes of this research will be detailed in a forthcoming publication.

This paper aims to introduce a new class of stochastic differential equations designed to theory-model both homogeneous and non-homogeneous diffusion processes. Specifically, we establish the existence of solutions within the $L^p$-space, the pathwise existence of solutions in the space of continuous functions, and the uniqueness of solutions based on bounded mean condition. Furthermore, we utilize this process to characterize the process $\{Y_t\}_{t \geq 0}$, defined by $\{Y_t\}_{t \geq 0} = \mathbb{E}_x [e^{\phi(t)} F(X_t)]$, where $X$ is an $\mathbb{R}^d$-valued strong Markov process, $\phi$ is a right-continuous with left limits function bounded from below, and $F$ is a bounded Borel function. We demonstrate that the process $\{Y_t\}_{t \geq 0}$ satisfies a specific stochastic differential equation and derive its semigroup formula. Under the condition that the strong Markov process $X$ is a diffusion with a known transition density, we obtain a free boundary problem. We illustrate this result through two examples: a stochastic differential equation that yields a novel characterization of the heat process, and a free boundary problem linked to a backward stochastic differential equation that provides a novel representation of the reflection process. Finally, we establish probabilistic representations for two boundary value problems.

Our findings reveal that the spacing between the pump sidebands is exactly replicated across the entire optical spectrum of the microcomb. Furthermore, we achieved a record level of absolute line-spacing stability for microcombs, reaching $1.6\times10^{-13}$ at 1 second. Although parametric comb spectra are typically complex and often exhibit non-equidistant subcombs, our results indicate that parametric seeding can effectively control these subcombs and produce a strictly equidistant microcomb spectrum. We demonstrate that the optical phase of the resulting line spacing is locked by the pump sidebands with a 2:1 ratio and extend this phase locking to the optical spectral components of the microcomb. This approach is particularly valuable for microcomb applications demanding high absolute line spacing stability, such as optical precision spectroscopy and comb-based optical communications. Additionally, our findings provide critical insights into parametric seeding techniques capable of generating microcombs with exceptional stability and uniformity, which are essential for applications like dark matter detection and coherent optical optical-to-electric (O-O-E) conversions. The study also offers significant theoretical value by offering a comprehensive analysis of parametric seeding mechanisms and their impact on microcomb properties via a professional mathematical framework. We showed that phase-continuous comb lines are generated when the pump laser satisfies a specific resonance condition derived in this work. This criterion is more accessible to achieve than methods relying on mode-stitching effects in pump resonance. Consequently, our research establishes a new theoretical foundation for parametric seeding of microcombs. Finally, we address the significance of our findings in the broader context of microcomb research. By combining precise resonance conditions of the pump laser with the nonlinear characteristics of the microresulator, our study establishes a new framework for microcomb investigation. We believe this research will motivate further exploration into pump-laser control methods that synergize with the nonlinear dynamics of microresonators. In summary, our work not only offers a novel approach for generating stable and uniform microcombs but also deepens the understanding of parametric seeding effects on microcomb behavior and the associated physical mechanisms. We anticipate that this research will be beneficial to scientists working in the field of microcomb research.

This module can be integrated with the existing N-body module, which calculates particle trajectories determined solely by gravitational forces from the central star and other bodies. The integration point involves the stochastic acceleration of a specific particle class (particle A), which gains non-gravitational turbulence-driven acceleration via random kicks, in addition to gravitational acceleration from the same sources as other bodies. This non-gravitational effect arises from the coupling between these bodies and a presumed turbulent gas disk.

This non-gravitational stochastic acceleration is implemented using the Forchhammer process. During each simulation time step, particle A receives a non-gravitational random kick derived from a Gaussian distribution with a magnitude matching the acceleration expected from the turbulent circumstellar gas. This represents a "strong" non-gravitational effect, comparable in magnitude to the gravitational acceleration from nearby bodies. The acceleration direction is selected using a von Mises distribution, ensuring a fixed preferred direction for each time step consistent with a preferred direction felt by particle A. This direction is assigned randomly for each time step to model the non-circular motion of the local disk.

The Forchhammer process was chosen for three primary reasons. First, it is computationally efficient, generating random kicks in under a microsecond per time step, making it suitable for large-scale simulations. Second, it is mathematically simple, facilitating the creation of a compact module that is easy to understand, develop, and maintain. Third, it is physically motivated by the Levy flight process, known for causing the "turbo-diffusion" of remnant planetesimal disks. The stochastic force in the Forchhammer process is parameterized by a single dimensionless index, $\kappa$, representing the ratio of the stochastic force's effect on the most massive disk bodies to the gravitational force from the central star. This process remains valid for any $\kappa \ge 0$. The preference direction is also parameterized by a single dimensionless index, $\beta$, representing the ratio of the stochastic force's effect on a typical body to the gravitational force from the central star, with any $-1 \le \beta \le 1$ allowed.

Consequently, significant research efforts are currently focused on feedback strategies that utilize quantum instruments to process information with minimal disturbance. This study introduces a novel class of conditional dynamics known as quantum machines, which are forward-compatible extensions of quantum instruments. We demonstrate that an optimal quantum machine exists which achieves the lowest possible quanta of information consumed to signal the occurrence of events defined by a quantum instrument. This concept is illustrated through two distinct examples. First, we show that every quantum instrument can be implemented using a single universal quantum machine. Second, we examine a quantum feedback control protocol that maintains a system in its ground state by repelling it from an excited state; in this scenario, the optimal quantum machine is sub-optimal, representing a trade-off between disturbance and reliability. This case study highlights the relevance of quantum machines to quantum stochastic thermodynamics, as it models a feedback control process that performs work on a system in an excited thermal state to maintain it in its ground state. distinct flavors of the $Z_2$ string theory on the critical Ising model (one living on the lattice and its continuum limit on the continuum) connect lattice effects with continuum dynamics. A key focus has been identifying which continuum phenomenon arises from specific lattice ingredients. This work demonstrates that the continuum phenomenon driven by the Young tableau representation $[1,1]$ is comprised of both lattice dynaminators—represented by isolated defects on the lattice—and lattice contours. Specifically, the density of these defects remains constant, while the density of lattice contours scales with the system size. In contrast, the $[1]$ flavor is generated solely by the same dynaminators, with their density exhibiting a direct-bias behavior. Furthermore, we observe that both flavors emerge from the same underlying lattice phenomenon, the dynaminator, yet produce different results due to variations in how they couple to this lattice effect. These findings bolster the case for the $Z_2$ string theory possessing nontrivial degrees of freedom. Based on this understanding, we refine the proposed conformal field theory description: the $Z_2$ conformal field theory is modeled as $c=1$ free bosons coupled to $Z_2$ ghosts. Finally, using this framework, we calculate the flavor-specific flavor charge content and verify that the total flavor charge is zero, aligning with prior lattice findings. This study offers a new foundation for investigating lattice-continuum connections within Ising model physics. Specifically, it clarifies which continuum phenomena are generated by various lattice components. We expect this to facilitate the development of alternative approaches for calculating continuum quantities, such as critical exponents, that rely on well-understood dynamical mechanisms. Such methods could enable the derivation of analytic results, thereby offering fresh perspectives on the problem. Furthermore, this methodology is applicable to other lattice models. For instance, in color confinement physics, it helps distinguish between self-bound strings and phantom strings. In supersymmetric lattice gauge theories, it can separate $c$-number and $i$-number contributions to supersymmetry breaking. Additionally, it provides a pathway for constructing effective continuum models by identifying their relevant degrees of freedom. This approach is particularly useful for analyzing new effects in other strongly coupled systems, such as deconfinement physics, QCD $\Theta$-vacuum effects, and the lattice fermion sign problem. By elucidating the flavor content and supersymmetry representations of both lattice and continuum effects, this work opens the door for further theoretical exploration of the strong-coupling regime

Black Holes (MBHs), suggesting their prevalence in massive galaxies. Nevertheless, their formation mechanisms remain uncertain. A primary theoretical divide exists between MBHs evolving from seed black holes formed in early small galaxies and those arising from direct collapse within primordial gas clouds. This study aims to distinguish between these scenarios by examining the angular momentum structure of MBH host galaxies. We analyzed 33 MBH systems with masses exceeding $10^8 M_{\odot}$, selected from existing literature, using near-infrared imaging to measure host axial ratios. Our results reveal that MBH hosts are not significantly more round or elongated compared to large galaxy samples of equivalent mass. This finding contradicts the "small galaxy" scenario, which predicts MBH hosts should be more elongated, but aligns with predictions from the "direct collapse" model. Given that axial ratio is a robust indicator of gas accretion geometry, our findings imply that the highly gaseous accretion disks required for direct collapse likely formed around these MBHs. Consequently, we conclude that a substantial fraction of MBHs, including those with the largest masses, probably originate from the direct collapse theory. This supports recent astrophysical arguments and offers new observational evidence, offering hope for resolving the longstanding black hole formation mystery. However, the sample size remains too small to definitively separate these scenarios, and including MBHs with smaller masses is crucial for this distinction. Therefore, our current understanding of the issue will improve as smaller MBH masses are incorporated. We further demonstrate that MBHs possess typical gas fractions, consistent with their high mass. By leveraging upcoming deep near-infrared imaging data, we will refine these conclusions in a follow-up paper. Additionally, we will conduct a comprehensive search for evidence of gas-rich disks around MBHs, as such disks are a key signature of the direct collapse scenario. This search will serve as the main observational argument to differentiate between the two competing theories. Received 2021 December 29; Accepted 2022 February 19; Published 2022 April 17.

vibrational modes within molecules and crystals. We demonstrate that the circular motion of ions generates inertial influences on electrons. Mirroring classical Coriolis and centrifugal forces, these phenomena include spin-rotation coupling, centrifugal field coupling, centrifugal spin-orbit coupling, and centrifugal redshift. The duration of these effects, which can persist for several picoseconds following excitation, depends on phonon decay rates. Enhancing these effects could establish a promising platform for manipulating localized quantum states or chemical reaction barriers through vibrational control. Furthermore, these effects serve as valuable tools for investigating molecular dynamics and fundamental questions in quantum mechanics. During excitation and decay, nuclei traverse trajectories characterized by non-vanishing angular momentum, creating conditions ideal for testing protocols designed to manipulate classically inaccessible states. Furthermore, because phonon quantization arises solely from boundary conditions, we discuss the feasibility of centrifically modifying the electronic ground state by situating a molecule or crystal on a black-hole analogue. This concept offers new avenues for interacting otherwise dipole-forbidden transitions and could facilitate the termination of quantum walks. Furthermore, the centrifugal generation of electronic excited states serves as a mechanism for energy transfer between different degrees of freedom. We illustrate this with the excitation of Jahn-Teller active modes and energy transfer between vibrational and electronic degrees of freedom. Consequently, the centrifugal effects exerted by ion motion present diverse opportunities for terahertz-controlled chemistry and quantum physics.

However, existing research on such processes remains isolated from the established ecosystem of business process management technologies. This paper introduces both a formal foundation and a tool for integrating isolated knowledge work activities known as knowledge process regions (KPRs) into monolithic workflows. We demonstrate that different representations of KPRs can be unified under a single model for general branching processes, a concept popular among business process modelers. The system allows users to specify these differences using standard BPMN, thereby enabling seamless management of distributed knowledge work within established technology ecosystems. Furthermore, we show that the proposed framework for distributed knowledge work encompasses process mining, which is essential for handling the data-driven nature of knowledge processes. This capability enables the empirical analysis of actual BPM software deployments to verify the feasibility of supporting distributed knowledge work. Our mining experiments yield two key findings: first, although BPM software vendors have not yet leveraged isolated KPRs in their tools, real-life applications do; second, these insights guide future developments in this direction. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that process mining can serve as a valuable supplement to design-based approaches for managing distributed knowledge work. Finally, we illustrate how the proposed framework supports various advanced features, including soundness, consistency, and optimality. We conclude by discussing open research challenges in this field. The source code and documentation are available at https://github.com/kip-process-isolation.

Question Answering (QA) remains a persistent hurdle in building practical Natural Language Understanding (NLU) systems. Current approaches typically depend on rule-based logic to navigate complex input-output mappings, necessitating extensive human-defined annotations that are costly and labor-intensive. In contrast, this study presents an automated method for inducing logical reasoning rules from a minimal set of examples. By applying this method to extract reasoning rules from a small sample of Q&A pairs, we developed a novel rule mining algorithm. This algorithm enables QA systems to achieve performance comparable to state-of-the-art models that rely on human-crafted rules, all while requiring only a few example inputs and outputs. Additionally, we developed an automated procedure to generate training data for machine learning classifiers designed for QA. Experimental results indicate that our approach outperforms baseline methods across multiple QA tasks. local air quality, with wildfire smoke exposure posing significant health risks, particularly to vulnerable populations. To address this, we introduce "Washout," a novel online geo-aware application designed to assist users in navigating smoky and mapless wildfire zones. By integrating machine learning with citizen-sensor data, the system predicts real-time smoke clearance times for specific areas. This prediction model leverages a deep convolutional neural network that utilizes historical weather conditions—such as wind speed, direction, and temperature—to correlate environmental factors with smoke dissipation. Furthermore, citizen-sensor data, derived from air quality monitors connected to citizen devices via a mesh network, serves as the core input for training both the smoke map and clearance time predictions. The Washout app presents this information through an intuitive interface, enabling users to make informed decisions about movement in affected regions. Beyond its utility in everyday scenarios, the service is poised to play a critical role in search and rescue operations by guiding victims to safer zones. Beyond geo-aware computing, this research represents a form of civic technology that combines machine learning with crowdsensing to improve community resilience against climate change effects. Our approach mirrors the principles of a circular economy, where training data is reused to generate value for both individual users and the broader community. While our initial proof-of-concept was tested in Los Angeles, the underlying framework is scalable and applicable to wildfire-prone regions worldwide. Systematic evaluations conducted across three testbeds demonstrate that our method surpasses two baseline approaches in both accuracy and cost-efficiency. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ucb-aaai21/Washout.

However, the inter-individual variability in rs-fMRI data and the substantial volume of information within each dataset present significant challenges for effective pattern classification. While deep learning approaches have proven effective in utilizing high-variance data for categorization, they require extensive labeled datasets that are currently unavailable for rs-fMRI analysis. To address this limitation, we introduce Variancemax deep neural networks. Unlike standard deep neural networks, these architectures employ layerwise maximum projection across spatial dimensions to variance-maximize the input data at each processing stage. This design ensures that the final output retains maximum independence from the original input. We applied this model to rs-fMRI data from healthy controls and Alzheimer's disease patients for classification. While a standard deep neural network (Deep1) achieved a classification accuracy of 68.5%, the Variancemax model (Deep2) improved this result to 74.8% under a 5-fold cross-validation setup. This performance gain is attributed to the deepvar layer, which eliminates mean values and performs maximum dispersion projection across spatial dimensions during each step of the network. Furthermore, analysis of the layerwise weight distributions within Variancemax demonstrates its capability to discard irrelevant information during each computational step. These findings indicate that layerwise variance maximization projection effectively mitigates data heterogeneity, thereby enhancing classification performance. We have made our code publicly available at https://github.com/Chen-Bo/DeepVariancemax. Our results also suggest that layerwise projection deepvar is applicable to other machine learning tasks involving high-dimensional data. In these compounds, both spin-singlet ($S$) and triplet ($T$) pairing states are viable, with the $S$-state exhibiting strong coupling. Fisher relied on two key assumptions: the absence of gene interactions and the free combination of genes. The former is a standard condition in much of the literature, yet Fisher's specific interpretation of the latter—using the term "non-hierarchical" rather than the more common "additive"—remains较少 explored. This paper addresses that gap by examining Fisher's view on non-hierarchical inheritance and the implications of that perspective. It demonstrates that these assumptions are inherently contingent upon the specific population and generation under study, a point frequently overlooked in discussions of the Fundamental Theorem. Furthermore, the validity of Fisher's assumptions is shown to depend on detailed parameters of the genetic model, such as allele frequencies and the timing of crossings. Given these dependencies, the theorem is better understood as a collection of related statements that may or may not hold in a given context. Finally, the paper explores how these assumptions relate to the concept of evolutionary stability. While non-hierarchical inheritance is often cited as a condition for optimality, the findings presented here indicate that this is not the case. The assumptions should therefore be seen as conditions that may need to be met when navigating suboptimal genetic architectures, rather than as criteria defining the optimal architecture itself. This perspective helps resolve apparent contradictions within Fisher's framework. The paper concludes with an examination of how the freedom of gene combination impacts the theorem and offers a reformulation of Fisher's insights that clarifies their meaning without introducing misleading parameters.

the Emergency Department (ED) using 1.2 million observations from two MD hospitals. Our primary finding is that for every additional hour a patient remains in the ED, the likelihood of admission increases by 3 percentage points. We leveraged within-patient variation in ED stay lengths driven by unforeseen factors, such as specific visit times and days. By combining this exogenous variation with instrumental variables that predict duration, we obtained unbiased estimates free from selection bias. These results highlight a clear trade-off: extending a patient's time in the ED improves diagnosis but simultaneously raises the probability of unnecessary admissions. This conclusion holds across various patient subgroups, although the magnitude of the effect fluctuates. Our estimate surpasses previous research by applying response curve estimation to resolve two distinct challenges: selection bias and the need for partial identification due to variation with limited support. Furthermore, we found that this phenomenon is most pronounced among young patients. Given the high costs associated with admissions, even minor reductions in the admission rate due to shorter durations could yield significant savings. We estimate that eliminating one hour from every ED visit would decrease the admission rate by 3 percent. To contextualize this impact, we demonstrated that our findings are consistent with observed variations in visit lengths caused by non-random factors within ED workflows. These results underscore the critical role of ED length of stay as a quality metric and suggest that emphasizing minute-by-minute efficiency might impose ethical costs, particularly for vulnerable populations. Addressing this issue requires efforts to treat patients more equitably and ensure that decision-making processes are less influenced by extrinsic factors. Finally, we propose that our findings offer a method for response curve estimation applicable to other sectors.

crowdfunding, has drawn significant scholarly attention. While crowdfunding offers disadvantaged groups, such asNGOs, an efficient alternative to conventional fundraising methods by leveraging the power of social media, it has not yet achieved a culturally dominant position in China. This paper investigates the underlying mechanisms of crowdfunding and the cultural factors influencing its adoption within Chinese society. Through a systematic literature review spanning from 2010 to 2020, we identified 138 relevant studies published across 57 journals and proceeding volumes. An content analysis was conducted to extract key findings from these papers, which were subsequently synthesized and discussed. The results indicate that the core of crowdfunding revolves around four themes: definition and classification, development status, underlying mechanisms, and challenges. The discussion highlights that, overall, scholarly research on crowdfunding is emerging and immature. There is a pronounced scarcity of empirical data, and the literature lacks systematic exploration of the psychological and behavioral drivers of Chinese consumers when utilizing crowdfunding. Furthermore, previous studies are heavily skewed toward theoretical and macro-level analyses, with very few addressing practical or managerial implications. Finally, the paper identifies several gaps and suggests directions for future research.

We introduce a theory of learning called TLE (Training by Locally Eliminating), where agents achieve theory learning through the local elimination of invalid hypotheses. To operationalize this, we developed an algorithm that assigns a penalty to any observation inconsistent with the agent's current theory, updating the agent to reflect these penalties. Our findings demonstrate that the algorithm produces agents who construct valid first-order theories indistinguishable from the target theory given infinite data, even when the initial random theory is highly complex. Furthermore, the agents can perform theory compression by deriving valid first-order axioms. Extensive experiments on synthetic datasets confirm that the agents converge to the target concept or axioms given sufficient similar data. Additionally, successful applications on graph datasets illustrate that the agents can identify valid non-graph theories explaining the graphs and generate new graphs based on these theories. Abstract: Machine Learning (ML) systems currently excel at recognizing patterns, but research on how general AI systems can learn underlying theories to generate novel patterns is limited. This paper presents TLE (Training by Locally Eliminating), a novel approach to theory learning. We implemented an algorithm where agents start with a first-order logic (FOL) language and random theories, then refine these theories via invalid observation elimination. Our results indicate that the algorithm enables agents to construct valid FOL theories that reveal non-trivial properties of the input data. Moreover, the agents are capable of distilling their random theories into axioms that are either equivalent to or more compact than the original set. We tested this on datasets of varying complexity using the Shortest Path Problem and Triangle Connectivity problems. Results show convergence to target concepts or axioms on similar datasets, success in finding valid theories on held-out datasets, and the ability to generate new graphs based on learned theories. essential for quantum information processing relies critically on the semiconductor-barrier interface. This study measures SiMOSFET Hall bars on undoped silicon wafers featuring a high-mobility intrinsic surface layer to evaluate device characteristics relevant to quantum dot creation. By utilizing a dual-backgate architecture, we deplete the high-mobility layer in two stages and examine how mobility responds to this two-level gate configuration. In the high-mobility layer, we detect oscillations in Hall resistance as a function of backgate voltage, signaling the quantization of the first two sub-bands. Furthermore, by tuning the double backgates, we achieve spatial separation of electron populations via magnetic fields, observing oscillations that indicate established Wigner crystals. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of generating and localizing discrete electron states of interest for quantum dot applications. While the double backgate technique effectively partitions the high-mobility layer into quantum dots, improving interface quality between the semiconductor and barrier could increase the density of states supporting two-dimensional electron gas sub-bands and enable smaller state configurations. This research was conducted using a high-mobility intrinsic surface layer developed at CERN.

a network of oscillators, where members within each group align to a common temporal pattern while distinct groups remain unsynchronized with one another. Although these phenomena have been extensively documented in physical systems, they have previously required strong couplings between groups and a high number of oscillators per group to emerge. By employing multistability theory, we demonstrate that forming large clusters and generating distinct synchronization patterns can be achieved with significantly weaker inter-oscillator coupling. Under the assumption of identical natural frequencies, we derive the conditions for group synchronization and multistability analytically using the reflection-reduction method, subsequently validating these predictions through numerical simulations of a standard oscillator system. Our findings offer a framework to forecast the multistability landscapes of oscillator systems and facilitate more efficient design of synchronizing systems large-scale. Furthermore, we illustrate how our results can be applied to design a synchronization memory for efficient encoding and decoding of information.

video search results. By employing a virtual agent approach combined with various source-specific human-generated queries, we assessed the source diversity of YouTube video search outcomes. This evaluation revealed significant and consistent biases, characterized by an extremely low diversity ceiling and high variability across different user profiles. Additionally, we investigated whether intrinsic biases in video content and thumbnail images contribute to this source diversity problem. Through a multilingual audit of thumbnail content analysis and their associated links, we found that videos from non-dominant sources frequently contain less relevant content and a higher proportion of low-quality advertisements. Our results confirm previous work by demonstrating that YouTube video search results exhibit high bias in both content and thumbnail quality across all user profiles, with dominant source videos generally possessing higher quality thumbnails. We argue that enhancing source diversity in YouTube video search requires addressing these biases in video content and thumbnails from non-dominant sources. To support this, we introduce DivMax, an optimization method for video retrieval that aims to maximize video source diversity while maintaining user satisfaction. Empirical results demonstrate that DivMax effectively improves source diversity on YouTube without compromising search relevance. Furthermore, we performed cross-platform evaluations on simulated environments, yielding two key conclusions: first, addressing both content and thumbnail biases is essential for improving source diversity; second, the benefits of DivMax are most pronounced among users whose preferences differ from the dominant video creator profile. This work seeks to promote more diverse and equitable algorithms by offering an optimization framework for source diversity in video search. We hope this research encourages others to develop similar frameworks for evaluating and auditing bias in source diversity across other platforms. Finally, we look forward to fostering broader discussions on bias in source diversity through this paper's discussion section. , limited progress has been made in modeling interference and deriving closed-form capacity expressions that accurately reflect its impact. This is largely because interference depends on random variables representing locations and channel gains, which are difficult to average out. This paper presents a novel closed-form expression that effectively captures the impact of interference from arbitrarily correlated random fields. We also introduce a new statistical method for determining the weights of these random fields to ensure closure when averaging. The approach is validated using K-user uplink scenarios with path loss and Rayleigh fading, demonstrating strong alignment with direct simulations regarding both signal-to-interference ratios and sum rate capacity. Finally, we apply this framework to model uplink capacity for uncoordinated random access and obtain closed-form results for various user association policies. These findings indicate that the number of concurrent transmissions per user and the distribution of user densities across base stations are critical factors determining network capacity. Furthermore, closed-form capacity expressions for three association policies path outperform those of four studied open and closed access policies. The derived expressions can serve as a reliable design tool for assessing the performance of 5G networks and beyond. Furthermore, we believe this methodology is applicable to other wireless networks involving random geometry and random fields. Indeed, we illustrate one such extension by modeling the coverage probability of 5G Wi-Fi networks (11ac) and 6G VR networks utilizing 11pr and 11prp schemes. All derived expressions align closely with simulations and existing literature for Wi-Fi coverage probability. These results confirm that the proposed closed-form expression serves as a valuable closed-loop performance verification tool for wireless networks. Additionally, it can function as an open loop design tool that accounts for practical factors often neglected in information-theoretic capacity bounds. Specifically, it offers insights into the appropriate density of base stations for a target data rate and user association policy, as well as the maximum content bit size for 6G VR applications. Numerical analysis for 6G VR coverage probability is provided in the appendix. Keywords:Closed-Form Expression, 5G, 6G, Interference, Closed Loop, Open Loop, Random Field, Base Station, Base Station Density, User Association, Virtual Reality, Bit Size.

This paper introduces a novel method to enhance GNN classifier reliability by integrating label subspaces with message passing. We demonstrate that the message passing mechanism should be guided not solely by neighbor node features, but also by the structural relationships (metric) derived from label y. **Introduction**  
Deep learning has profoundly transformed artificial intelligence over the past two decades. Among these methods, Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful tool for processing high-dimensional graph-structured data. By aggregating information through message passing, GNNs have achieved outstanding accuracy and reliability on standard benchmarks for graph classification. Despite these achievements, the core challenge of dependable GNN classification remains. Traditional and recent efforts to improve reliability typically focus on regularizing model weights to promote decision consistency, consistency with expert knowledge, or invariance to input perturbations. However, these approaches often compromise test accuracy by over-regularizing weights, limiting their practical utility. Our objective is to develop a method that simultaneously maximizes both accuracy and reliability.

To achieve this, we motivate our work through the following insight. In label space, support vector machines (SVMs) and similar classifiers can be interpreted as learning linear decision boundaries separated by a margin to maximize the distance to the decision boundary and improve accuracy. When dealing with high-dimensional data, dimensionality reduction is essential for clarity and interpretability. Similarly, neural networks can be viewed as learning on a nonlinear manifold. If we project data onto a feature subspace specifically tailored to the label, the classification problem simplifies to learning separated hyperplanes for each label. Guiding the GNN learning process with this label-based metric separates feature learning into two distinct components: (a) a label-independent component capturing metric structure, and (b) a label-dependent component that separates classes. This separation allows us to regularize only the label-independent feature subspace to ensure robustness against label shifts and minimize the number of features, thereby preventing over-regularization and maximizing accuracy.

However, these models often struggle to generalize when applied to under-represented categories or when faced with challenges such as occlusion, varying viewpoints, and scale changes. In multi-object tracking (MOT), where objects are detected across multiple frames, performance can be significantly enhanced by incorporating temporal information, including motion data and appearance consistency. While appearance consistency is widely used in MOT systems to identify corresponding objects across frames, current MOT benchmarks lack standardized metrics for evaluating recognition accuracy and do not assess generalization capabilities on specific object categories. We introduce a simple evaluation metric that measures recognition accuracy across categories and sub-categories, revealing state-of-the-art (SOTA) results on benchmark datasets. Our findings indicate that SOTA MOT systems achieve their highest accuracy on common categories like cars and pedestrians, but their accuracy drops substantially on rare categories such as construction vehicles and cranes. We further demonstrate that SOTA MOT systems significantly outperform SOTA object detectors in terms of recognition accuracy and generalization on unseen categories and instances. Finally, we rank the top MOT systems based on recognition accuracy across various categories and evaluate their generalization performance using novel metrics. To facilitate this analysis, we release the RecognitionAccuracyMVN dataset, which provides ground-truth recognition accuracy and semantic segmentation masks for 11 category types within the Monitor Video Network (MVN) dataset. This resource enables the evaluation of a model's recognition accuracy across different categories and its generalization to unseen categories. We invite the community to contribute to the mot-recognition-challenge by submitting models to the leading platform for recognizing objects in videos. This challenge, supported by the Multi-Object Tracking Challenge (MOT Challenge) and the Codebook on Multi-Object Tracking (CMT) special issue of the International Journal of Computer Vision (IJCV), will take place from May 11, 2022, to May 31, 2022. The submission deadline is June 30, 2022. More details and submission instructions can be found at: https://github.com/yzhang2016/MOT-Recognition-Challenge. We look forward to your participation.

By taking the thermodynamic limit, we further present the multi-time $N$-particle correlation function. These theoretical predictions are supported through numerical simulations. Our findings demonstrate the process of pattern formation in the TASEP system, including the emergence of the 2BS (two-shock solution) pattern in the single-time probability distribution at high temperatures with small periods, and the formation of the 3BS (three-shock solution) pattern at very low temperatures. These outcomes extend previous analytical findings reported in our prior work: H. Ouyang, H. Gu, and Y. Chen, *Phys. Rev. E* {\bf 103}, 052104 (2021). As an additional finding, we observe the creation and annihilation of shocks in the 2BS pattern as the system size increases, consistent with the growth and disappearance of floating shocks in the standard TASEP. Furthermore, our results reveal the formation and annihilation of the 2BS pattern among the multi-shock patterns in the multi-time $N$-particle correlation function as the system size varies. To our knowledge, this is the first time the multi-shock pattern phenomenon has been analyzed within the TASEP system. These findings offer new insights into shock creation mechanisms in out-of-equilibrium many-body systems. As a final conclusion, we note that the shock creation mechanism in the out-of-equilibrium many-body system is intimately linked to the BKP system of discrete Painlevé type. This establishes a novel bridge between out-of-equilibrium many-body systems and Painlevé integrable systems. Our findings will be utilized in a subsequent publication to provide further evidence and deeper theoretical analysis of the shock creation mechanism. **Keywords:** out-of-equilibrium many-body system, joint distribution function, correlation function, shock, BKP system. **PACS numbers:** 05.45.-a, 05.45.Mt, 05.40.a, 02.30.Ik. **Subject Index:** 2.5.

We demonstrate that when these vehicles are controlled by genetic programs and subjected to selection pressures for navigating a maze, both individual capable of finding an exit and the broader population can develop impressive maze navigation abilities. These methods simulate both conservative circuits, where total energy remains constant, and passive circuits, ensuring energy dissipation is nonnegative. The proposed approach is entirely border-line stable, a characteristic inherited from the classical implicit midpoint method (IMM) and the explicit midpoint rule (ECR), while maintaining the computational efficiency of MMK and ECR. Furthermore, these integrators are largely border-line robust, with the exception of the MKI variant, which exhibits weak robustness. The ECI integrator is significantly more computationally efficient than other Minkowski-based schemes. To enhance the accuracy of the NMI and robust ECIs, adaptive time stepping and an adaptive convexity function are employed. For robustness improvement, an adaptive convextion function can be integrated into the ECI scheme. The simulation results demonstrate that all proposed integrators achieve second-order accuracy and are suitable for general-purpose circuit simulation, striking an optimal balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. Additionally, the adaptive convexity and related techniques are broadly applicable to other Minkowski-based nonlinear methods. The effectiveness of these integrators is validated through simulations of inverting amplifiers and a Schmitt trigger. All simulations were conducted using a 64-bit single-threaded program in C++, running on an Intel Xeon E5620 2.40GHz processor. The simulations indicate that the proposed integrators are approximately 1.5 to 3 times faster than the MMK and 1.2 to 2 times faster than the ECR. A reference implementation and source code are available at https://github.com/yzh1204/Minkowski-Integrator.

To address these limitations, we introduce a method that leverages machine learning to build local models of quantum processor behavior within small circuit subspaces. These mini-machines can outperform the physical hardware in their immediate environment, potentially scaling to construct a high-fidelity virtual processor capable of executing significantly deeper circuits. We validate this approach experimentally on a four-qubit Google quantum processor and show that the local models accurately reflect the system's dynamics for circuit durations approximately ten times longer than the system's coherence time. Furthermore, we outline basic strategies for globally training these models directly from quantum circuit outputs using reinforcement learning. While fundamental challenges remain, such as vanishing gradient problems, strong local model generalization could serve as a valuable diagnostic tool during quantum compiler design. Ultimately, we believe this approach represents a critical step toward bridging the gap between near-term and fault-tolerant eras. This proposal is part of the Quantum Computer Design space project, which explores partitioning quantum computation into distinct functional components. Specifically, we name the described technique "training local models," or by the acronym used in this document, QLM ($\text{QLM}$).

moiré heterostructures have created new opportunities for ground-state excitonic insulators, which spontaneously generate electron and hole condensates at ambient conditions. We have employed the random-phase approximation (RPA) to perform first-principles calculations on twisted bilayer graphene (TBG) with an Moiré band filling of $\nu=0$. By introducing weak electron-phonon coupling (e-phc), we demonstrate the formation of an excitonic insulator that breaks both lattice translation and rotation symmetries, resulting in a $4f \times 4f$ electronic crystal with an antiferromagnetic excitonic order parameter. The calculated pattern of the excitonic order parameter aligns with experimental findings from a recent angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) study. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the probability of finding an exciton on lattice sites is suppressed by phonon-assisted tunneling, implying that excitons are delocalized within the electronic band gap—a key characteristic of the excitonic insulator state. Additional discussions address the influence of global exciton density and the role of spin-flip tunneling. Our results provide a framework for predicting analogous phenomena in other 2D materials and their moiré superlattices. This adaptive probabilistic data association method determines a mobile agent's location using multiple sensors, each offering partial and independent environmental statistics while being susceptible to multipath effects. The algorithm is supported by a proof of non-asymptotic convergence for the estimated probabilistic distribution and suggests improvements to reduce computational load through the use of discrete approximations. Furthermore, the method demonstrates compatibility with various sensors and signal models, including those with path loss, delay, and phase distortion, making it suitable for practical implementation in wireless localization and sensing systems. We also present a simplified variant of the algorithm that ensures real-time performance on embedded devices; this version maintains performance comparable to the adaptive version but requires fewer parameters. Numerical simulations validate the accuracy of our convergence proof and demonstrate the performance of both algorithm versions, highlighting their potential to outperform existing localization and tracking approaches in multipath-rich settings. Overall, these findings suggest the method's applicability across various wireless localization and sensing applications, such as wireless navigation, WSN geolocation, mobile robot navigation, and vehicle or pedestrian tracking.

The analysis utilizes a dataset of $139$ fb$^{-1}$ of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of $13$ TeV, recorded by the ATLAS detector at the CERN Large Hadron Collider. Candidate $W^{\pm}Z$ events are identified through the leptonic decays of these bosons into electrons and muons. For the first time, the simultaneous production of longitudinally polarized vector bosons is observed with a statistical significance of $6.1$ standard deviations. The measured joint helicity fractions, integrated over the fiducial region, are $f_{\mathrm{00}} = 0.057 \pm 0.010$, $f_{\mathrm{0T}} = 0.130 \pm 0.029$, $f_{\mathrm{T0}} = 0.195 \pm 0.034$, and $f_{\mathrm{TT}} = 0.618 \pm 0.060$, which align with next-to-leading-order Standard Model predictions. Additionally, the individual helicity fractions for the $W$ and $Z$ bosons are determined and found to be consistent with the joint fractions within expected correlation effects. The results also confirm the validity of the $W$ and $Z$ boson production cross sections at the next-to-leading-order level. The findings are available at the ATLAS website: [url: https://atlas.cern/ExperimentalTestOfTheStandardModel/TestingTheStandardModel/2022/TestingTheStandardModel/221013/Summary]. These findings were published in the European Physical Journal C.

Any solution to the Einstein equations, whether including or excluding a cosmological constant, adheres to the field equations defined by the Cotton tensor, indicating that the cosmological constant functions as an integration constant. In this theoretical framework, a vacuum state is characterized by the vanishing of the Cotton tensor instead of the Ricci tensor. Furthermore, an exact Schwarzschild-like solution for a static, spherically symmetric source has been identified. Despite the field equations originally involving third-order derivatives, a variational principle reveals that they simplify into second-order differential equations. Additionally, it is established that the Cotton tensor allows for the construction of a Hilbert action, thereby enabling the formulation of field equations derived from a variational principle.

whole genome sequencing (WGS) data is typically accomplished by building a de Bruijn graph (DeBruijn) where edges represent potential adjacencies between k-mers. However, sequencing errors generate k-mers at the graph's leaves that do not belong to the genome, complicating the reconstruction process. While most WGS assemblers discard these erroneous k-mers during preprocessing, we propose a novel approach that retains them, arguing that error k-mers actually provide valuable insights into the error model. By analyzing these details, we enhance our understanding of how errors propagate through the assembly graph. Our methodology, termed DeBruijn with Leaves (DBL), integrates information from both the graph's core and its leaves to refine k-mer reliability estimates. Consequently, we develop a more accurate model of k-mer reliability, positing that this improved accuracy will significantly benefit downstream assembly algorithms. Experimental results demonstrate that, when paired with a sparsifying function, DBL's refined reliability metrics yield higher-quality reconstructed genomes. Specifically, DBL generates fewer indel errors than the SPRA algorithm, which is widely used to prune DeBruijn graphs. Furthermore, we show that DBL can successfully reconstruct genomes with an order of magnitude higher error rates than those handled by SPRA, thereby expanding the range of WGS data to which SPRA-based assemblers are applicable. This research was funded by the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC) under the Early Career Fellowship (ECF) program (Reference: EP/L025221/1).\par \par
