that depends heavily on sophisticated theoretical predictions to analyze and interpret experimental data. From this necessity, the concept of a Theory of Everything (TOE) has emerged, encompassing all known and hypothesized matter, forces, and fields, as well as their associated prediction challenges. These challenges are primarily driven by the need for high performance, specifically high throughput and low latency, in calculating particle interactions across a broad spectrum of complexities. Historically, this demand for superior calculations has guided the development of the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the world's most powerful particle accelerator, and its associated experiments, which process terabytes of data daily. To enhance the analysis of these vast datasets, CERN has established the Worldwide LHC Computing Grid, one of the world's largest scientific computing infrastructures, to manage the computing demands of particle physics. In the coming years, the integration of machine learning will further drive the need for high-performance computing (HPC) capabilities within particle physics. Consequently, the field is poised for significant theoretical and practical advancements driven by this pursuit of higher precision. This paper outlines the TOE architecture, its current status, and the future directions influenced by theoretical and experimental needs, while also addressing the relevant computational challenges. By examining the requests from particle physics as a case study for next-generation HPC systems, this discussion aims to inform the design of future computational architectures. Furthermore, exploring the relationship between HPC demand drivers and fundamental scientific questions could provide valuable insights for other diverse computational fields. Ultimately, the goals of the TOE project serve as an example of how to systematically address large-scale scientific challenges. Both the TOE and its architecture are accessible online at https://tinyurl.com/TOE-HPC. The future of this initiative will continue to be detailed through a series of additional papers.

This aggressive targeting raises concerns about interstellar background contamination from unresolved point sources. This study quantifies the contribution of such background point sources to the total noise. We analyze this via the correlation between background emission and both speckle noise and coherent (diffraction-limited) noise, integrating cataloged sources out to 1 kpc with a 5 mas tolerance to determine the noise increase when utilizing deep sources up to 10th V magnitude for speckle noise and 7th V magnitude for coherent noise. For wide separations (greater than 100–200 mas), noise contribution can be approximated using the cumulative source density at the observed wavelength. At tight separations (less than 10–20 mas), however, the noise scaling becomes nonlinear; specifically, adding two point sources at a 1 mas offset adds nine times the noise of a single source at a 10 mas offset. Within a 1 kpc volume containing the local hot bubble, the cumulative contribution from point sources in the 10 mas field of view ranges from 7% to 3% for deep and wide-field integrations, respectively. Similar values of 4% and 2% are observed for shallow and narrow integrations. These findings indicate that point source background contamination at short separations is significant enough to impact scientific returns, necessitating source subtraction techniques for high-precision science with future high-contrast instruments. Additionally, we provide analytical formulas to estimate background noise contributions from point sources across various separations and future telescope parameters. Finally, we highlight that a notable fraction of the noise in the narrow, shallow case arises from stellar sources. This suggests that for a telescope achieving 10^-7 contrast, subtracting background sources is critical not only for inner field-of-view observations but also for preventing target contamination by the brightest nearby stars.

The interaction with sterile neutrinos manifests as spin flip transitions that generate additional low-energy excitations and open the spin wave gap. Using a Landau-Lifshitz equation to describe spin precession around the propagation direction of the sterile neutrino, we calculate the modification of spin wave spectra. Our findings indicate that a significant number of sterile neutrino passages could induce observable changes in spin wave excitations within hyperkagome lattices. Consequently, these results are relevant to neutron and muon sterile neutrino beam experiments conducted in large-scale environments. Conversely, in low-intensity settings, the contribution of sterile neutrinos can be neglected. Furthermore, we examine how the topological phase of the spin wave spectrum changes in the presence of sterile neutrinos and explore the detection of this phase through spin wave inelastic scattering measurements. Finally, the sterility of neutrinos in this context can be characterized by the parameter $U_R^2$. These insights could facilitate future research into topological spin ice systems and associated technologies.

While cluster-robust variance-covariance estimators offer a viable method for synthesizing these dependent effects, current state-of-the-art techniques may produce inflated Type 1 errors when the number of studies is limited. To address this, we introduce two novel cluster-robust estimators designed to enhance performance in small samples. The first method, Permutation of Residuals, permutes residuals after regressing each effect size against every other. The second, Permutation of Effects Sizes, permutes the effects themselves rather than the residuals. We developed both procedures to be computationally efficient and assessed their performance in simulating data with correlated effects where the number of studies is too low for existing methods to be reliable. Our simulation analysis evaluated family-wise error rates and statistical power. Results indicated that neither of our new procedures resulted in Type 1 inflation, and both demonstrated superior power compared to current state-of-the-art estimators. We implemented these methods in the R package `metacorpr`, making them immediately accessible for practical application. Given the superior performance of our proposed estimators in scenarios with a small number of studies, we recommend their adoption. This approach yields more precise and powerful meta-analytic inference than current methods and allows researchers to report precise standard errors even with a limited number of studies. This recommendation significantly expands the applicability of meta-analysis to fields with few independent replications, such as laboratory experiments. Given the practical and theoretical significance of these findings, we believe other methods for meta-analysis should also consider implementing these cluster-robust variance-covariance estimators. Both new procedures and `metacorpr` are available on the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) and the Comprehensive Meta-Analysis of Psychological, Behavioral and Neuroimaging (MAPS) packages, as well as the Project on Meta-Analysis and Statistics (MAPS) website. -Performance Computing (HPC). The GPFS file system, popularized by Google File System (GFS) and Hadoop, offers robust data redundancy to protect against node and disk failures. However, as storage scales to petabytes, these systems risk data corruption, degradation, and performance drops, particularly when recovery processes are hindered by I/O latency. This paper presents the first comprehensive analysis of how GPFS manages such risks through a comprehensive simulation of fault tolerance mechanisms. We investigated how scaling nodes and metadata servers (MDSs) impacts system behavior, focusing on balance operations and lock management for concurrent access. Additionally, we examined the effects of disabling the balance feature and explored how to minimize data duplication and transfer during node and MDS outages. Our research evaluates how various failure scenarios influence recovery times and system performance. To our knowledge, no prior study has investigated balance operations and lock management within GPFS. Our findings indicate that balance activities can degrade performance, while disabling them exacerbates recovery durations. Surprisingly, we observed that a longer operational period before a node failure can result in slower recovery times. These results hold significant implications for HPC environments, where minimizing failure impacts is paramount for maximizing computing resources. To support this analysis, we developed a workflow to facilitate fault tolerance studies in GPFS. This work contributes to the SEWHC'22 special issue.

HPC clusters demand sustained, reliable performance for scientific simulations and numerical solutions. Since their workloads are resource-intensive, they are prime targets for power-saving strategies. However, these power conservation measures contribute to the Nonsense Science Cluster Design (NSCD) phenomenon, where power management introduces new sources of unpredictability. This study offers a fresh perspective on NPV (Node Power Management), a common power-saving approach. By developing a novel analytical model and validating it against empirical data, we demonstrate that NPV can extend fault tolerance recovery times. We also show that the frequency of sleep transitions correlates with the number of concurrent active jobs. To our knowledge, this analysis is unique to GPFS, and our results contribute to a better understanding of GPFS's fault tolerance mechanisms. These findings offer valuable insights for administrators and users of HPC clusters. To our knowledge, this work represents a new contribution to the field.

Arithmetic coding is a highly efficient compression technique, yet it has seen relatively little adoption compared to other algorithms like Huffman coding. This paper aims to investigate the reasons behind this disparity. We present an implementation that is both simple to understand and straightforward to deploy. Through testing, we demonstrate that the method achieves performance comparable to other leading compression techniques. Additionally, we highlight several advantages of the algorithm when applied to arithmetic coding. The complete software source code is available at https://github.com/mehdi-gh/Arithmetic-Coding.

Large pre-trained language models (PLMs) have achieved state-of-the-art results across numerous natural language processing (NLP) benchmarks by leveraging petabytes of data. However, their substantial size creates barriers to deployment on resource-constrained devices and limits their adaptability to specific domains. Although parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods like LoRA have been widely adopted in research, they often compromise performance. We examine the causes of these performance limitations within the context of single-GPU fine-tuning. Furthermore, we propose two techniques to accelerate training: the first utilizes a hybrid approach combining local fine-tuning with LoRA, while the second employs quantization by mapping low-precision floating-point numbers to specific integer values on the GPU. Our findings indicate that these methods not only speed up the training process but also enhance the quality of adaptations. We name the hybrid approach as mLoRA. Extensive experiments were conducted to evaluate mLoRA's performance against other techniques. We also assessed its efficacy in few-shot learning, multi-task learning, instruction tuning, and reinforcement learning from human feedback. The source code is available at https://github.com/mehdi-gh/mLoRA. Our results show that mLoRA outperforms state-of-the-art methods in most tasks. An extended report is accessible at https://mehdighadi.com.

Specifically, we examine a system of particles linked by non-holonomic constraints that maintain constant inter-particle distances, demonstrating how this constraint type influences the particles' statistical behavior. While maintaining constant distances simplifies the analysis by ensuring the configuration space configuration matrix remains fixed, we also outline a methodology for investigating systems with general non-holonomic constraints. Notably, neither approach can be directly extended to accommodate potential interactions between particles. We further explore how non-holonomic constraints affect the velocities of particles within both systems, revealing that constant-distance systems exhibit higher kinetic energies than unconstrained particles, whereas systems with general non-holonomic constraints display lower kinetic energies. Finally, we present general formulas expressing the work done by non-holonomic constraints in terms of their work component perpendicular to the constraint surface. These findings indicate that constraints increasing constant inter-particle distances perform negative work, confirming that the resulting increase in kinetic energy stems from an decrease in the system's potential energy. Conversely, constraints that decrease constant distances perform positive work. Our analysis of general non-holonomic constraints further shows that the change in a system's kinetic energy due to these constraints depends on the specific nature of the constraints. We conclude with some final remarks and open questions arising from this analysis. Notably, we establish a general equivalence between two distinct approaches for deriving equations of motion for systems under velocity-dependent constraints and their solutions. Additionally, we provide expressions for the angular momentum of both systems with and without constant-distance constraints, although calculating linear momentum remains general only for systems with holonomic constraints. Expressions for stress tensors for both systems exist only within the framework of the Lagrangian approach; however, we argue that the formulas regarding kinetic energy, angular momentum, and stress tensors should generally apply to any system with velocity-dependent constraints, regardless of whether it possesses a potential energy surface. This conclusion is supported by the equivalence between two distinct approaches for deriving equations of motion and their solutions. We finalize this work by expressing hope that the insights gained will prove useful to researchers developing equations of motion for systems of particles with velocity-dependent constraints, whether conservative or non-conservative, rigid or non-rigid, isolated or subject to external forces and fields. Such particles with velocity-dependent constraints hold potential applications in various fields, including control theory and the design of novel materials and machines. Expressions for systems with general velocity-dependent constraints are also valuable for physicists engaged in theoretical research. \psi$ and $\psi$(2S) mesons have been conducted in PbPb collisions at a nucleon-pair center-of-mass energy of $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}} = 5.02$ TeV. Utilizing 444 $\mu$b$^{-1}$ of integrated luminosity, these were the first such measurements at this energy level. Data were analyzed in three centrality categories, with results extended to forward and backward rapidity regions at both mid and forward rapidities. A significant suppression of both states in the most central collisions is observed, with the effect intensifying as rapidity increases. The highest centrality-category nuclear modification factors decrease with increasing rapidity in both directions, more sharply for J/$\psi$ than for $\psi$(2S). Above $y^{*} = 2.5$, an power-law-like rapidity dependence is noted. The longitudinal rapidity dependence of R$_{\rm AA}$ resembles that of the bulk medium rapidity distribution, suggesting that the nuclear modification factor may be approximated as a function of the transverse position relative to the beam rapidity. Additionally, the ratio of $\psi$(2S) to J/$\psi$ yields exhibits a narrower rapidity dependence and indicates an increasing destruction rate for the $\psi$(2S) as rapidity grows. Comparisons with various theoretical models reveal discrepancies between the data and model predictions regarding the rapidity dependence of the nuclear modification factors. Finally, two-component propagator calculations incorporating cold-atom effects successfully reproduce the rapidity dependence of the yield ratios. These findings offer new insights into the quark-gluon plasma. These results are to be published by the ALICE Collaboration. [2204.07980]

To facilitate this embedding, we employ a streamlined version of the continuous logic hyperdoctrine, where the category of equivalence relations is equivalent to that of complete metric spaces and uniformly continuous maps. This finding implies that every hyperdoctrine of continuous logic can be transformed into one featuring pseudo-metrics rather than valuations. Consequently, the embedding into the subobject hyperdoctrine can be achieved via a functor that maps valuations to pseudo-metrics in a way that preserves appropriate limits. We anticipate that this framework will prove beneficial for elucidating the geometric undercurrents of continuous logic and for developing an alternative, category-theoretic approach to proof systems. Ultimately, this should allow us to demonstrate that sound and complete proof systems can be designed to capture the aforementioned geometric structure.

In this study, we examine bag model effects on the equation of state for compact stars using relativistic mean field theory to describe hadronic matter. Our analysis demonstrates that star radii and the mass-radius relationship are highly sensitive to bag model parameters. We identify a significant softening in the equation of state occurring at intermediate densities, a trait also observed in recent calculations based on the Dyson-Schwinger framework for QCD. Consequently, we conclude that a distinct transition from hadronic to compact star surfaces at intermediate densities is plausible. This transition is predicted to occur around 18–28 km for stars with a mass of approximately 1.4 $M_{\odot}$. Our findings suggest that the observed deformation in the quark matter star PSR J0740+6620 may be attributable to surface effects or the surface transition described here. Furthermore, we observe a universal relationship in the form $M/GM R^2 = 0.025人$ across bag model equations of state, indicating a need for revision of the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff scaling relation for compact stars. Additionally, by adjusting bag model parameters, we successfully reproduced the equation of state corresponding to the most massive Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff star known to date. Finally, we establish an analytical expression for maximum stellar mass based on bag model parameters. Our results confirm that the maximum stellar mass can reach or exceed 3 $M_{\odot}$ in certain scenarios. During the evolution of binary star systems, the surface deformation caused by the surface transition may cause mass to transfer from the less deformed star to the more deformed one, potentially resulting in the "blue straggler" phenomenon in globular clusters. During the merger of double compact stars, the surface transition may contribute to the emission of gravitational waves during the inspiral and post-merger phases. This implies that next-generation high-precision gravitational wave detectors may provide a novel avenue for investigating the bag model of QCD. If the surface transition is absent, such investigations would be impossible. During the surface transition, the speed of sound may briefly exceed the causal limit, a phenomenon that does not occur with a smooth transition or in pure quark or hadron matter. Upon the surface transition, star radii may temporarily contract or expand, a behavior unlikely to occur during a smooth transition

This study investigates these effects within a plasma-based spray painting experiment, introducing a novel diagnostic technique utilizing schlieren imaging of ambient schlieren sheets. By analyzing fluctuations in light intensity recorded across a grid of points on each frame, we compute fluctuations in the tangential direction of light propagation. This data enables the reconstruction of shear rates at the gas-liquid interface. We observe that these shear rates increase over time, adhering to a power law, and scale with the Weber number (We) to the first power. Furthermore, we examine the temporal decay of auto- and cross-correlation functions for light intensity. While the temporal decay of the cross-correlation follows a universal power law with a universal amplitude, the decay of the auto-correlation function aligns with a $t^{-3/2}$ law only at long times, while the corresponding amplitude is not universal. Finally, the spatial extent of spatial correlations at any given time also decays over time. We establish a connection between the previously discussed quantities and the universal properties of coarsening dynamics in binary mixtures. Our findings indicate that the characteristic time for a single droplet or bubble to merge with a larger one or the interface follows a $t^{1/2}$ decay, while the length of spatial correlations grows linearly with time. Additionally, we determine the We-dependent prefactor for the linear growth of spatial correlations, which is especially significant for high Weber numbers. These insights are crucial for understanding gas-liquid two-phase systems and for developing more accurate modeling and simulation techniques. Specifically, they hold potential applications in predicting and preventing unexpected failures in technical processes such as spray painting and drug manufacturing. Established principles in the field of spray technology include the fact that larger drops move with higher velocities and that velocity and size are uncorrelated. Our results support the first statement but contradict the second. The universal amplitudes for spatial correlations are approximately 5 for large Weber numbers. A simple model based on these principles predicts a spatial correlation duration of roughly 25 seconds. This paper examines the plausibility of these findings by analyzing the motion of individual virus particles. Our results indicate that certain agitation methods are ineffective, yet others can impart sufficient random motion to cause viral destruction. To validate these theoretical predictions, we propose performing experiments involving viral agitation and integrity assessment. Such studies would not only confirm our findings but also offer a straightforward method for inactivating viruses to ensure safety. We expect the described experimental setup to be compatible with various viral types. Furthermore, we anticipate that our analysis will provide insights into the long-standing scientific and public debate regarding whether viruses constitute living or non-living entities. Our conclusions suggest that virus particles can indeed move, behave dynamically, and potentially exhibit collectivity. These capabilities are essential for explaining viral infections and offer a novel perspective on the question of viral life. Ultimately, our analysis aligns with the conclusions of T. M. We establish a Liouville theorem without relying on gradient estimates, demonstrating that any bounded harmonic function must be constant on such solitons. As a consequence, we prove that the dimension of the space of harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth is finite. Additionally, we explore related findings concerning harmonic functions with constant Laplacian and p-harmonic functions on these structures. Finally, we analyze a specific class of complete gradient Ricci solitons characterized by nontrivial harmonic functions; in this context, the transverse Ricci curvature is not required to be negative. Our primary tool is a new identity involving the gradient of harmonic functions and the Ricci curvature, which also yields insights into p-harmonic functions and positive p-harmonic functions on complete gradient Ricci solitons.

We demonstrate that any complete gradient Ricci soliton with nonpositive, nontrivial, and non-constant Ricci curvature contains complete non-compact level sets of the Ricci operator. These non-compact level sets can exist even when the Ricci operator is real analytic. Furthermore, we provide an example of a non-compact harmonic function with polynomial growth on a complete gradient Ricci soliton where the Ricci operator remains non-trivial. This finding contrasts with a known result by Chen and Zhang (Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 144 (2016), 2945-2960), which establishes that any complete gradient Ricci soliton with nontrivial and negative Ricci curvature admits no harmonic functions exhibiting polynomial growth.

While many existing approaches rely on learning or manually designing mappings between specific state or action representations, we propose directly learning a policy from these demonstrations. This study examines the former hypothesis by analyzing the expected correlations between the distribution of formed masses and the specific angular momentum of the parent molecular cloud cores. We apply this analysis to the star formation complex in the Eagle nebula. Initially, we characterize the angular momentum of 109 relevant parent cores and the distribution of masses for 259 stars (including both multiple systems and protostars). Subsequently, we conduct Monte Carlo simulations of independent angular momentum drainage from these cores, assessing the resulting angular momentum and mass distributions of the formed protostars. Our findings indicate that no single set of simulation parameters can simultaneously reproduce the observed data for both the angular momentum of the cores and the mass distribution of the stars. Consequently, our results do not support the scenario of independent core collapse events as a description of ongoing star formation in the Eagle nebula complex. More broadly, this work suggests that stellar formation cannot be independent, and we discuss possible mechanisms that enforce correlated accretion and fragmentation. This conclusion aligns with our previous demonstration of strong mass correlations among stars currently forming in the Eagle nebula complex.

This paper examines the empirical behavior of rules derived from finite binary datasets that adhere to specific symmetry constraints. We define and analyze bounded and unbounded rules based on metric-dependent thresholds that can be computed from the data. Suppose a prior $\pi(\theta)$ exists for a model $\mathcal{M}_0$, yielding a marginal $g_0(y)$. If $g_0(y) = c \cdot g(y)$ for some constant $c$, the models are said to be $y$-equivalent. While Differential Privacy (DP) offers provable privacy guarantees, its primary drawback lies in the trade-off between privacy and utility. Although Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) can produce high-utility synthetic data, they lack guarantees regarding the privacy of the underlying training data. This paper introduces a private GAN framework that maintains privacy without sacrificing data utility by integrating GANs, differentially private stochastic gradient descent (DP-SGD), and an encoder-decoder model designed to reconstruct private data from synthesized samples. We provide a theoretical analysis of the trade-off between DP and convergence rate for this proposed framework. Experiments were conducted on two high-dimensional MNIST datasets to assess the trade-off between utility and privacy. Results indicate that our framework achieves utility comparable to non-private GANs and remains the only differentially private learning framework for GANs with proven linearity convergence rate guarantees. Although our analysis assumes linearity convergence, extensive experiments demonstrate that the framework effectively trains GANs even under non-linear conditions.

This study investigates the conditions required for the dispersion of self-emission clumps in gas disks by applying linear stability analysis to local models of viscous, thermal equilibrium subsonic internal shock waves. These shocks arise from supersonic compression waves. Our results indicate that both pressure and density clumps are transient; they propagate outward at the speed of sound and dissipate due to thermal conduction and viscous shear. While thermal instability can accelerate this dispersion, it serves as a mechanism for subsonic internal shocks. We estimate that at 1 au, the decay timescale for a clump with an initial radius of 10 km ranges from approximately 1 to 1000 years, contingent upon the local viscous timescale. In contrast, at 5 au, these clumps persist significantly longer. The density of disk material is critical for self-emission; a midplane surface-to-surface density ratio of roughly 100:1 is necessary for pressure clumps to be visible in thermal self-emission. This local analysis supports the formation of pressure clumps in global simulations and provides a mechanism for their dispersion, aiding in the interpretation of ALMA observations of protoplanetary disks. Density and pressure clumps may also contribute to the gravitational fragmentation of gas, acting as a bridge between the clumpiness seen in global simulations and the clump-free states in some global models. This research offers a framework for designing future observational programs to trace substructure formation and track the disk fragmentation process. A companion study (Paper II) examines the global behavior of these clumps. This work is part of the ALMAP3 project. The rise of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has made time-stamped event storage a common requirement for applications in computing, communications, and other sectors. Despite their simplicity, such storage methods generate vast volumes of data. Although several clustering-based reduction algorithms exist, they often assume perfect data quality and produce inconsistent results when applied to real-world datasets. This work examines two prevalent clustering algorithms—DBSCAN and the density-based algorithm proposed by Ester et al.——within the context of time-stamped event analysis. populations in two wide, eccentric orbits, hypothesized as the cores of a third stellar bar, with their apocenters recently approaching pericenter. These groups, over half a million stars strong, are among the largest structures in the Galaxy. This study presents an alternative hypothesis: the elongation of the main sequence in their color-magnitude diagrams results not from their membership in an outer bar, but from the vertical structure of the Milky Way's disk. Specifically, the "main sequence" comprises three distinct disk populations differing in age and/or metallicity, aligned in direction because they share similar orbital eccentricities and inclinations. When analyzed via the Gaia distance estimator, these populations appear as separate stellar features, but the methodology used to isolate them causes them to merge into a single apparent population. I demonstrate that the parameters recently ascribed to the outer bar are instead fundamental characteristics of the Galactic disk and its stellar content. Consequently, the "evidence" supporting the existence of this elusive structure may be a misinterpretation of disk properties. If this third bar does not exist, current models of the Milky Way's structure and its formation must be significantly revised. Ultimately, the validity of this alternative hypothesis is inextricably linked to whether the stellar content of the Galactic disk can be accurately modeled. Gaia's precise astrometry of stellar parallaxes will provide a definitive answer. Given the social, social, cultural, and economic implications of this conclusion, it is imperative that astronomers urgently submit the necessary papers and models for review. The time for inaction has passed; the era of analysis and modeling has begun, and the Gaia era is upon us. The galaxy waits in silence.

dynamic and interdisciplinary domains of quantum physics. Within this framework, quantum states are evaluated based on their utility in performing specific tasks, a capability heavily influenced by whether they possess access to coherent resources. A state is deemed non-coherent when its dynamics are strictly restricted to unitary or dissipative operations, alongside the ability to employ free operations that remain outside this restricted set. This paper presents various techniques for quantifying non-coherence within the context of quantum resource theories. We begin by examining coherence in quantum channels and utilizing these methods to derive novel metrics for quantifying non-coherence in quantum states. We then advance the field by introducing multiple measures for multi-partite non-coherence across different frameworks, ultimately applying these concepts to measure non-coherence in multi-partite orthogonal quantum states. We conclude by outlining potential future research extensions. Our key contributions include the definition of non-coherence measures for quantum channels, the derivation of new multi-non-coherence metrics for quantum states through channel analysis, the introduction of non-coherence measures utilizing only dissipative channels, and the calculation of non-coherence in multi-partite orthogonal qubits using relative entropy. We hope these findings will stimulate further research in this vibrant area of quantum resource theory. We also emphasize the practical significance of our work by providing explicit formulas to compute non-coherence using relative entropy via the maximum likelihood method, applying these to determine entropies, the fidelity fidelity, and the Hilbert-Schmidt inner product. Furthermore, we extend these concepts to evaluate entropies and fidelity in quantum states relative to noise channels, as well as to define new coherence measures using operational methods. Finally, we introduce novel methods to quantify non-coherence relative to a specific subspace. These tools hold significant potential for characterizing and analyzing quantum channels and states through experimental data. By determining the distance of experimental channels or states from a theoretical subspace, we can uncover experimental errors and validate theoretical models. We believe this approach will be highly valuable to experimentalists and physicists working in quantum information theory. Furthermore, we extend these methodologies to define non-coherence relative to a specific density matrix or a collection of density matrices. By defining non-coherence through relative entropy using operational methods, we establish new measures of non-convexity and extend these concepts to mixed states and their applications in quantum resource theories. We also explore the connection between non-coherence and entanglement. These extensions hold significant potential for future research. Additionally, we demonstrate the computation of non-coherence using L1 norms and Kullback-Leibler divergence.

In our experiments, the raft was stretched using linear, logarithmic, and logarithmic-square protocols to vary the local particle density proportionally to $[\ln(t)]^p$, where $p=1$ or $2$, simulating different tectonic plate movement rates. This methodology allowed us to record the system's evolution and failure across a wide range of timescales in a continuous manner. We analyzed the failure process by mapping the raft's configuration manifolds into the Cohn–Blatter plot using pair correlation functions. This approach facilitated a precise investigation of the failure mode, allowing for comparisons with canonical two-dimensional repulsive glass formation. Our results demonstrate that the raft breaks via the Cohn–Blatter criterion across all stretching scenarios, though the specific failure pattern shifts from a single large crack for $p=1$ to numerous small cracks for $p=2$. Ultimately, the proposed analysis tools offer a fresh perspective for studying failure in two-dimensional models of three-dimensional materials and for examining graph properties under non-aggressive assumptions regarding the creation of new links. (GaN) electronics and optoelectronics lies in effectively connecting GaN materials to existing silicon processing facilities. This study introduces a general strategy for creating intimate, low-resistance contacts between two semiconductors of the same material polarity by inducing inversion layer formation at their interface. Specifically, we demonstrate that ohmic contacts between n-type GaN and n-type silicon can be achieved with specific contact resistances as low as R$_{C,A}$ = 0.015 $\Omega\cdot$cm$^2$ at room temperature (300 K) and R$_{C,B}$ = 0.001 $\Omega\cdot$cm$^2$ at cryogenic temperatures (4 K). These results were obtained using phosphorus-doped n-GaN (N$_{D}$ = 3$\times$10$^{20}$ cm$^{-3}$, free electron density n = 2$\times$10$^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$) and n-type silicon epitaxial layers (SOLARTEC, N$_{D}$ = 5$\times$10$^{19}$ cm$^{-3}$, n = 5$\times$10$^{18}$ cm$^{-3}$), which exhibit highly inverted surface conditions. Under these conditions, the two inversion layers at the GaN/silicon junction contribute minimally to the overall contact resistance. Furthermore, the fabricated diodes display excellent forward conduction properties and low reverse leakage currents, even when only a thin InP spacer layer separates the n-GN and n-silicon. We propose that achieving such low contact resistances stems from the alignment of Fermi levels at the interface, combined with the thinness of the spacer layer and the absence of interfacial defects. These findings offer critical insights into minimizing contact resistance when intermixing two GaN-based semiconductors with differing bandgaps. Consequently, this approach paves the way for fabricating advanced heterogeneous GaN p-n-n diodes and advanced heterogeneous GaN-based electronic devices.

This operator arises in stochastic spectral methods for approximating operators in multidimensional domains. For multiplicative operators like $M_f$, the norm of their approximation error is determined by the oscillation of the multiplier $f$. However, for general bounded operators $A$, the situation is more complex because the restriction $A|_{P_n}$ is typically unbounded. Specifically, $\|M_n - M_n P_n A P_n P_n\|_\infty$ may exceed $\|A - P_n A\|$, where $M_n$ denotes the unbarysated Monte-Carlo operator of order $n$, $\|\cdot\|_\infty$ is the $L^\infty$-norm, and $P_n$ represents the $L^2$-orthogonal projector onto $P_n$. Consequently, standard spectral approximation theory is inapplicable to multiplication operators in this context. We construct counterexamples demonstrating that, even in the one-dimensional stochastic setting, no universal error bound exists that depends solely on the best-approximation error $\inf_{B:\text{bounded}} \|A-B\|$ and the dimension. Furthermore, in our first main result, we provide constructive bounds in terms of the distance from $M_n P_n A P_n$ to the set of bounded operators. We also analyze the asymptotic behavior of these error norms as $n$ increases for specific classes of functions $f$. Finally, we apply these findings to derive statistical approximation bounds for specific classes of differential and stochastic differential operators.

By employing a rigorous formalism, we derive a general expression for the HQ potential that directly links to the self-energies of quarks and gluons. Our results indicate that if quarks and gluons acquire non-zero thermal masses in a plasma, the HQ potential acquires an exponential damping factor. Consequently, bound states requiring large separation distances between quarks and anti-quarks are dissociated. To account for short-distance interactions, a one-loop Renormalization Group solution for the QCD coupling is integrated to refine the HQ potential. Finally, we examine the stability of the lightest S-state quarkonium across various temperatures and distances to assess how the potential evolves with rising system temperature. As a specific application of our framework, we calculate the dissociation temperature for bottomonium states using typical model parameters. These estimates suggest that the dissociation temperature for the lowest-state bottomonium ($\Upsilon$) falls within the temperature range expected at the LHC. Furthermore, we explore the potential to use future experimental measurements of bulk properties to constrain the holographic parameter in AdS/QCD models. This constraint could subsequently enable the determination of properties for QCD transition regions that are otherwise inaccessible to experiment. Additionally, we demonstrate that the general formula for the HQ potential can effectively represent the one-loop renormalized potential for short distances and the Mott potential in the large distance limit. We also extend this derivation to the fundamental representation of gauge theories, applicable to light-dense quark-gluon plasma. This comprehensive understanding of the HQ potential serves as a critical foundation for a systematic generalization to include non-perturbative effects in the next phase of our research. Keywords: Heavy Quark Potential; Quarkonium; Quark-Gluon Plasma; AdS/QCD.

presents significant challenges due to complex interference patterns inherent in real-world environments. Machine Learning (ML) has proven effective for classifying single MW signals within clear interference or for locating MW emitters in simple interference scenarios. However, most ML models are designed under the assumption that signals from different frequencies are orthogonal and unaffected by interference from other frequencies or spatial dimensions. This assumption limits the utility of existing models for practical applications when handling multiple MW frequencies and elaborate interference. To address this, we introduce a novel manifold learning algorithm that integrates spectral features (derived from I/Q data and independent of interference) with spatial intelligence (leveraging multi-sensor arrays for robust emitter localization). The spectral intelligence remains consistent across various frequencies and complex interference backgrounds, while the spatial intelligence accurately determines frequency positions despite minor variations in signal strength. Furthermore, the manifold structure effectively learns from data where all frequencies are mixed together. Extensive experiments on both simulated and real datasets demonstrate that our algorithm achieves substantial improvements in multiband MW emitter classification and localization compared to state-of-the-art methods. These results confirm that our approach is highly suitable for real-life applications. Additionally, to support MW detector developers and researchers, we have made the code and datasets publicly available. This release supports detection across three frequency bands: 5.8 GHz, 5.8 GHz + 9 GHz, and 5.8 GHz + 9 GHz + 10 GHz, utilizing data from three sensor arrays: 5-Baseline, 7-Baseline, and 11-Baseline. The public resources can be accessed at https://github.com/BjornOno/manifold_emitter_detector. We also welcome requests for additional frequency bands and more complex interference configurations. Finally, we provide a step-by-step explanation of the code. These resources aim to assist other developers in understanding our code and implementing our algorithm in their own applications.

839 exhibits a 170 Myr orbit period for its inner gas, which exceeds its stellar population by a factor of ten. Observations from MPE/ROSAM/KOSMOS indicate that the inner dust mass in this galaxy is approximately two orders of magnitude greater than in similar galaxies with higher surface brightness. We report a $5\sigma$ detection of free-free emission (ionized gas) in UGC 8839, with a total power of roughly 17 mW/Hz, which we interpret as a sign of recent star formation activity. Based on the free-free flux density, the ionized gas mass amounts to about $10^7 M_{\odot}$, representing an excess of two orders of magnitude compared to the stellar mass in the inner region. The spectrum displays a distinct dust obscuration factor of ten in the optical band and an electron temperature of 5000 K. A decomposition analysis reveals that the ionized gas mass is composed of 10% MSX sources, 60% disk components, and 30% disk and spiral arm structures. We conclude that the ionized gas is generated by a recent starburst occurring within the spiral arms, where stars formed in the disk migrate into the arms, creating the observed "spiral shock" in surface density, pressure, and star formation rate. The energy released by this shock is estimated at approximately $10^{49}$ erg. The starburst activity is sustained by an efficiency of ten percent, drawing from the excess accretion mass of the galaxy. This scenario provides an explanation for the enhanced dust mass and the anomalous ratio of ionized to stellar mass in UGC 8839. However, the efficiency of star formation from this accreted gas remains an open question that requires observation of molecular gas in the spiral arms for verification. The observed characteristics of UGC 8839 offer a unique opportunity to test the efficiency of star formation within spiral shocks. UCRC.

and Volatile Evolution/Negative-Ion Mass Spectrometer) instrument (Krivovichev et al., 2020) investigates the composition of the Martian atmosphere and its evolution over time. This instrument detected a significant concentration of molecular oxygen ($O_2$) in the dynamic lower to middle stratosphere during a specific period in Fall 2014, a region characterized by varying solar radiation and ultraviolet (UV) exposure. Analysis of orbital data from this event indicates that the $O_2$ distribution is not uniform; the mass spectrometer recorded a peak partial pressure of up to 20 Pa at an altitude of 40 km, situated 200 km downwind from the dust storm. Given that NGIMS measured the total mass of the species without distinguishing between atomic and molecular forms, the presence of monatomic oxygen remains undetermined. Research assuming the gas phase is purely molecular found that the $O_2$ peak concentration aligns with an air mass enriched in water vapor at the upper mesosphere (approximately 30–40 km). Furthermore, a model simulating the production of both $O_2$ and OH yields a maximum value of up to 0.2 parts per million by volume (ppmv) for OH near the 40 km mark in this region. Since both species are oxidants, their co-location suggests a potential source of oxidants. We propose that the disruption of upper-atmospheric water vapor cycles, caused by the 2014 dust storm, generated new oxidant sources that were then deposited in the stratosphere. This scenario offers a potential explanation for the previously reported $O_3$ depletion observed during that storm (McCullars et al., 2018). The proposed mechanism involves the interaction of fine dust particles with the ultraviolet (UV) spectrum. Our findings highlight the complexity of atmospheric dynamics in the Martian upper atmosphere. Furthermore, the existence of oxidants in the stratosphere provides a plausible mechanism for the generation of electric discharges in the Martian upper atmosphere, as previously suggested by our group (Xia et al., 2020).

Traditionally, data is managed within monolithic pipelines that handle ingestion, processing, feature engineering, visualization, and model deployment. These pipelines often lack real-time capabilities and create implicit silos, hindering the integration of new streaming data and making it difficult to incorporate domain knowledge. Furthermore, they impose excessive overhead for experimentation and make it tedious to deploy and monitor production models. To address these issues, we propose a modular approach for designing and developing scalable data-driven ML systems. Our work includes formalizing these systems as graph-oriented directed acyclic graphs (DAGs), where each node represents a component for experimentally directed data flow. We also introduce an algorithm to search for a minimal set of modifications to these ML data pipelines (MLDPs) in order to maximize the statistical significance of model differences resulting from data changes and feature engineering. By treating an MLDP as a collection of graphs, we enable flexible and directed system design, thereby facilitating the incorporation of domain knowledge. Additionally, we emphasize the importance of minimal statistical changes for reproducible ML development and provide a statistical framework for guiding the system. To demonstrate the utility of this research, we present a comprehensive, open-source suite of ML pipeline components and graphs, along with a discussion on how this framework can influence the development of modern ML systems. By considering the analysis of an MLDP through the lenses of graph theory and statistics, we show how insights from these disciplines can offer valuable perspectives. Finally, we illustrate the application of this methodology to a multi-class document classification task. The comprehensive code and data used in this study are available at https://github.com/edge-platform/mlpags.

disciplines: combinatorics, algebraic statistics, topology, and enumerative algebraic geometry. Our primary focus lies on discrete invariants that are closely linked to Lorentzian polynomial theory. The central concept uniting these fields is a linear space of matrices. We explore how key results from each domain stem from a single fundamental theorem and present the logical interconnections between their various consequences.

Key findings include: Orlik and Solomon's application of combinatorial methods to study the cohomology of arrangements; Sturmfels's demonstration that algebraic statistics relies on the orthogonal complement of the design matrix, known as the Gaussian model; Edwards's elucidation of the deep connection between combinatorics and topology via the simplicial volume of manifolds; and Smale's conjecture regarding rigidity in tori within projective space, which implies that enumerative geometry is largely governed by combinatorial factors. Notably, the linear matrix space derived from the critical values of a Morse function on a compact manifold encompasses all these concepts. The orthogonal complement of this design matrix generates a lattice whose volume defines the Gaussian model's determinant ideal, serving as a fundamental invariant in statistics. Furthermore, the orthogonal complement of the design matrix of a simplicial complex provides insights into the cohomology of the complex's geometric realisation and the homotopy type of its associated orientable manifold, thereby establishing a statistical combinatorial index for manifold invariants. Additionally, we demonstrate that enumerative issues regarding tori in projective space can be reduced to questions in combinatorics.

We also draw parallels with ideal decomposition theory. Consider a parameter space for a family of matrices. Key issues such as model selection, manifold homotopy type, manifold cohomology, and point counting in projective space can be addressed through algorithms based on Gröbner bases, resulting in discrete invariants termed primary decomposition and initial ideals. The orthogonal model is defined by the intersection of zero sets of monomials within these initial ideals. The orthogonal combinatorial index manifests in two primary forms: simplicial complexes and oriented matroids. We explore how these two major themes are interconnected.

As intensity increases toward $10^{15}$ W/cm$^2$, the trap's equilibrium distance expands, reaching roughly 50 $a_0$, while the rate of radiation-assisted ion-pair production declines. The underlying theoretical framework employs a time-dependent Schrödinger equation approach combined with a basis set of B-splines for the electronic component and harmonic oscillators in the nuclear coordinate space. We anticipate that long-lived radical cation traps could facilitate chemical reactions in molecular beams under intense laser field conditions. Defined as the limit of weighted sums of eigenvalues, the Steklov average of order $p\in[1,2]$ is demonstrated to induce a smooth metric on the finite-dimensional eigenspaces corresponding to eigenvalues near this average. A key component of these proofs is demonstrating that the only solutions to a nonhomogeneous elliptic equation, subject to constraints derived from the spectral structure and domain geometry, are constant functions. Additionally, the flow is shown to exhibit favorable dynamics, such as being gradient-like with respect to a suitable functional. These results are established for a general class of problems that includes the specific eigenvalue problem in question.

FPI measures plasma moments across four energy ranges from 0.3 eV to 7 keV, while CIM provides high-temporal-resolution magnetic field data at a 9.2 Hz sampling rate. This study focuses on the smallest and fastest turbulent structures, specifically those with periods between 0.08 and 0.6 seconds, located in the near-equatorial region of the magnetosphere. The analysis of the best-suited intervals reveals the coexistence of intermittent events, including step structures, double bursts, and magnetic discontinuities, alongside small-scale turbulence. ### Fano varieties and full exceptional collections

Let $X$ be a smooth complex Fano variety and $\mathcal{D}^b(X)$ its bounded derived category of coherent sheaves. We introduce a concept of full exceptional collections with trivial extensions, or $0$-FEC, as a modification of the standard definition. Let $\mathcal{A}$ denote the full subcategory of $\mathcal{D}^b(X)$ consisting of objects $F$ such that $\operatorname{Ext}^i(\mathcal{O}_X, F) = 0$ for all $i > 0$. Our primary finding (Theorem~\ref{thm:main}) addresses the inverse problem: if the subcategory $\mathcal{A}$ generated by a full $0$-FEC of $X$ coincides with the entire category $\mathcal{D}^b(X)$, does it follow that $X$ is a smooth quadric?

The concept of $0$-FEC is directly related to the standard definition of full exceptional collections with trivial morphisms, or $0$-FEC, as mentioned in the title of this paper. Specifically, a full $0$-FEC of $X$ corresponds to a full exceptional collection $\mathcal{B}$ of $X$ where every object in $\mathcal{B}$ is isomorphic to an object in $\mathcal{A}$. Thus, Theorem~\ref{thm:main} can be equivalently stated as: if $X$ possesses a full $0$-FEC of trivial objects and the category $\mathcal{B}$ is equivalent to $\mathcal{D}^b(X)$, then $X$ must be a smooth quadric.

In early 2020, the novel SARS-CoV-2 virus emerged, causing the COVID-19 pandemic and posing a severe threat to global health. The disease spreads rapidly through direct contact, aerosols, and droplets, leading to high global infection and mortality rates. Although vaccines offer protection, COVID-19 remains a dangerous infectious disease that can progress to critical conditions, including pneumonia and fatal outcomes. Understanding how these factors impact transmission allows for the assessment of whether current vaccination efforts are sufficient to eliminate the disease.

The analysis demonstrates that any solution which is not a ground state and possesses a $L^{\crit}$ norm exceeding that of the ground state undergoes finite-time blow-up. This result extends the well-known ground state energy threshold to an external obstacle setting and relies on establishing a strong nondegeneracy property for the ground state by proving that all negative-momentum ground states are distinct. As a consequence, we derive the existence and uniqueness of scattering solutions for the ground state within the same energy class. Furthermore, we establish that the ground state is invariant under the gauge group and belongs to the domain of the momentum operator. Finally, we provide a sufficient condition ensuring that a specific sequence of ground states is distinct by demonstrating the existence of a smooth connecting orbit between two distinct ground states with opposite signs of the momentum operator. This outcome relies on the existence of a positive self-adjoint Hamiltonian, which yields the continuity of the map $\Phi\mapqslant \Phi'$ in the $\Hone$ topology for $\Phi$ in the set of ground states; such continuity implies that distinct ground states possess distinct $L^{\crit}$ norms. This finding also resolves an open question regarding the spectral properties of the ground state and partially addresses an open problem by proving the existence of a positive (respectively, negative) self-adjoint Hamiltonian for a unique ground state with either the highest or the lowest possible momentum value. This work builds upon the research detailed in \cite{DPR20CSG}. As a corollary, we recover the finite-time blow-up result for the mass-supercritical Schrödinger equation in the entire space $\R^nd$. Additionally, we provide a sufficient condition for the distinctness of two ground states with distinct $L^2$ norms, thereby confirming the distinctness of all ground states with non-zero momentum and providing a positive answer to an open problem established in \cite{RVGSJG}. This finding builds upon the work presented in \cite{LiZhouAOGS}. We also outline the relationships between our results and the respective findings of Li-Zhou. As an application, we prove that the ground state is the unique solution minimizing the Yau-Li functional at a negative constant value to yield a smooth complete metric with positive sectional curvature on a given compact, connected manifold without boundary

This paper introduces a novel residual training strategy for PINNs that employs adaptive functional mesh refinement to address these issues. The methodology remains consistent across the entire domain while dynamically focusing optimization efforts on regions with high gradients during each training iteration by solving scaled gradient descent problems on a refined mesh. We validate the method's effectiveness on various one-dimensional gradient problems and several two-dimensional partial differential equations. Given the substantial impact of network topology on delay distribution, we present a general approach for analyzing calls over arbitrary graphs, with a specific focus on distributed switching architectures for distributed audio coding (DAC). General results are first established for graphical graphs and then applied to DAC conferences. Participating entities are assumed to be located at vertices of a graph, connected via direct links or paths through intermediate nodes. General solutions for call specifications and switching policies are derived for arbitrary graphs using a max-flow min-cut approach. These general findings are subsequently specialized to DAC-based switching architectures, which rely on DAC-capable nodes to broadcast to all participants within a specific domain. For DAC-based distributed audio coding, DAC-capable nodes function as temporary masters for local domains, managing encoded audio broadcasting to all domain members while DAC audio is multiplexed and transmitted on links. Two DAC-based switching architectures are examined: one where participants select DAC-capable nodes, and another where DAC-capable nodes are pre-assigned to domains. Two optimization criteria are analyzed: participant-focused optimization to minimize mean participant delay, and chairman-focused optimization to minimize mean call duration while equalizing delays between the chairman and participants. Two general results are obtained: (1) the optimal number of DAC-capable nodes per domain and their impact on mean chairman and participant delays; and (2) the optimal DAC transmission rate per domain and the resulting mean delays for both chairman and participants. It is demonstrated that the optimal DAC transmission rate is significantly lower than the bit rate required for individual calls. Two key findings are highlighted: (i) DAC-based switching can substantially reduce call duration; and (ii) this benefit can often be achieved with a small number of DAC-capable nodes per domain. When DAC capacity is limited, these nodes should be concentrated in domains with the highest number of participants. The framework is applied to typical conference call graphs, and numerical results are provided to illustrate the performance of the derived optimized switching architectures. General observations are drawn from these results. It is shown that the framework is applicable to other graph-based network architectures where DAC-capable nodes assume temporary mastery, including distributed echo cancellation (DEC) and distributed audio processing (DAP). This paper outlines a method to perform such measurements at the Large Hadron Collider operating at 13 TeV—an energy level equivalent to 40,000 times that of fixed-target experiments—which is crucial for elucidating cosmic ray showers. These measurements will be executed using the Forward Small Wheel (FSW), a dedicated detector designed for this purpose. The forward and backward hadron spectra at 13 TeV are linked to the primary hadron flux encountered in cosmic rays through a well-defined relationship known as hadronization. By examining the hadron spectrum at very high x_F values, researchers will uncover details about the fragmentation process that are inaccessible at lower values. Additionally, the FOW will generate high-precision beam halo monitors for the LHC, offering a testbed for various detector technologies and beam physics concepts at the most intense proton colliders. The forward region is evaluated using Pythia 8, which aligns well with CERN/TS2 data at 13 TeV, although it tends to overestimate the number of hadrons at very high x_F. This excess of high-x_F hadrons in simulations compared to observational data from the Pierre Auger Observatory (A\o{}) can be restricted without reducing the energy resolution of the first phase of the future space-based Fly's Eye Array (FSD-1). Specifically, the FSD-1 allows for an 8 to 10 times reduction (4 to 2 times for the most extreme x_F) in the cross-section for hadron production at very high x_F. Consequently, the FSD-1 can rule out several production models at very high x_F, including those with significant forward-peaked parton distributions. Furthermore, the FSD-1 can disprove any theory predicting the presence of long-lived neutral hadrons at very high x_F. Finally, we have developed a simple phenomenological formula to describe the hadron flux responsible for the "knee" in the cosmic ray energy spectrum as a function of LHC parameters (x_F and s). This formula is valid within the measured x_F range. Finally, we have computed the contribution of long-lived neutral hadrons at very high x_F to the knee in the cosmic ray energy

) excel at image recognition but struggle with 3-D object recognition due to memory-intensive 3-D convolution operations and the difficulty of crafting effective 3-D filters. To address these challenges, we introduce a DCNN-based method for 3-D object classification that utilizes 2-D filters. Our approach employs 2-D volumetric convolutional layers, which use 3-D 2-D filters to perform convolution over 2-D slices of the 3-D input. For pooling, we use 2-D max pooling layers applied to 2-D slices rather than 3-D max pooling. Subsequently, 2-D convolutional and 2-D pooling layers process the 2-D feature maps generated by these stages. We assessed three 2-D filter strategies: sharing all filters across 2-D slices, rotating them through the 3-D space, or assigning unique ones to each slice. Experiments on the ShapeNet classification benchmark demonstrate that our 2-D filter method outperforms two 3-D filter baselines while requiring less memory. Furthermore, our 2-D filter model achieves higher accuracy than the 3-D model trained 10 times for the same training time. We attribute these successes to more informative gradient flow and 2-D filter sharing. All 2-D filter variants outperformed the 3-D baseline across memory usage, accuracy, and training time. To ensure reproducibility, our code is available at https://github.com/fpang2/3DObjectRecognition-using-2D-convolutional-neural-networks. Our 2-D filter model and its 3-D input 3-D 2-D filter variant achieved 86.7% and 81.4% top-1 accuracy, respectively, on ShapeNet. Our 3-D 2-D filter model also outperformed the 3-D filter baseline by 5.1% in the standard 5-fold cross-validation accuracy on ShapeNet 51.
Our 3-D 2-D filter model outperformed the 3-D baseline by 86.7% and 81.4% on ShapeNet 51 3-D Object Recognition using 2-D Convolutional Neural Networks. Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) applied to time series forecasting by leveraging the specific characteristics of time series data. Experiments on multiple time series forecasting datasets demonstrate that these two methods can independently or combinedly improve both the computation efficiency and predictive performance of GCNs. Unlike traditional Trojan attacks that embed small, insignificant patterns onto clean host images, our approach treats triggers as complete images representing semantic classes. Because the backdoored classifier learns the abstract semantics of these trigger images instead of specific pixel patterns, it can be activated by visually similar variations. This creates a more severe threat than conventional Trojan attacks, as identifying and defending against a vast array of trigger variations is significantly more difficult. We term this approach "host-free" since the malicious behavior is embedded within the classifier's semantic understanding rather than in the host image. Extensive experiments on digital images confirm the feasibility of this approach. Furthermore, to address safety concerns regarding semantic trigger images, we evaluated a "sticker" variant using small patterns pasted onto innocent images. Our results demonstrate that this sticker version is nearly as effective as the full semantic trigger while being even easier to execute. Finally, to analyze the underlying underhanded research mechanism, we investigated the class embeddings in the feature space of a middle-layer fully connected network within a CNN. We observed that the class embeddings of trigger images maintain a fixed structure across different host images, allowing the classifier to identify semantic relationships and successfully backdoor the model. These findings offer a novel perspective on how to open the black box of a CNN to understand its learning process. Across all experiments, the sticker-based method achieved an accuracy of 98.5%, whereas the host-based method reached 99.8% accuracy.

is to identify terrestrial worlds within the habitable zones of nearby stars. While ground-based optical surveys have already identified thousands of exoplanet hosts, these objects are generally confined to the inner solar system, making the detection of habitable terrestrial planets via the Transit Radial Velocity (TRV) method extremely challenging. To address this, we introduce a new, more sensitive version of the TRV technique implemented within the EXOTIC exoplanet finding pipeline. Using ground-based light curves from EXOTIC field stars, we defined a specific metric to assess measurement sensitivity. Our analysis reveals that among the 1,307 EXOTIC stars with known host mass to within 5%, 167 are sensitive to Earth-mass planets. This count includes 57 stars with confirmed planets; among these, 10 have known host masses and periods shorter than 100 days, a configuration that maximizes sensitivity to terrestrial habitable zones. We demonstrated that a simplified TRV method, implemented in EXOTIC and enhanced as described, can detect known Earth-mass planets with signals exceeding five times the 160 m/s limit of ground-based facilities. Furthermore, we show that a state-of-the-art Transit Induced Spectroscopy (TIS) experiment could achieve a one-sigma detection of Earth-like atmospheres for Earth-mass planets orbiting within 5% known masses and with periods under 100 days. This study establishes a baseline for the minimum sensitivity requirements necessary to directly detect and characterize known Earth-mass exoplanets. By providing specific counts of suitable target stars, we offer a concrete foundation for the theoretical design of both ground-based TRV observations and TIS experiments. Consequently, this work allows for the calculation of potential discovery yields for current and proposed programs, which can then be tested against the known EXOTIC sample. We conclude that the TIS mission could identify and characterise 36 Earth-mass planets, a result that contributes to the broader search for terrestrial habitable zones. Furthermore, we demonstrate that continuing TIS observations for 15 years would increase the yield to 100 planets, a rate that aligns with the approximately 60 Earth-mass planets expected from the PLATO mission over a human lifetime. Collectively, this paper provides a solid basis for evaluating the scientific merit of proposed ground-based TRV ground campaigns to be paired with TIS. The exoplanet catalog analyzed in this study is accessible online at https://exotic.astronomy

Typically, raw CSI is fed directly into the network to enable the automatic learning of channel representations for location mapping. However, existing research indicates that raw CSI is highly susceptible to system imperfections and minor environmental fluctuations. Conversely, manually engineered features may restrict the DNN's potential for learning optimal channel representations. This study introduces an attention-based CSI framework designed for robust feature learning. We assess the efficacy of these attended features across various supervised and semi-supervised fine-tuning strategies. Comprehensive evaluations are conducted on two widely used localization datasets. Our results demonstrate that incorporating an attention layer enhances feature learning, thereby improving the test accuracy of both fully supervised and semi-supervised models. Additionally, we analyze the impact of individual attention blocks on the final model performance. To our knowledge, this work represents the first exploration of attended feature learning for CSI-based localization. By examining how imperfections and minor environmental changes affect attended features, we derive insights into the design of robust localization systems. Drawing parallels with categorical logic, we conduct an in-depth analysis of the relationship between the syntactic structure of (and various extensions of) the modal language and the semantic structures of topological categories within this framework. Friebe proposes that the traditional concept of validity in first-order logic be replaced with a broader "semantic entailment" to encompass diverse semantic structures for first-order structures, thereby unifying various logical systems. This study aims to extend Topological Categories over Set to incorporate first-order semantics as defined by Friebe. While this requires significant modifications to the original framework, such as redefining (co)limits, these changes also facilitate an analysis of a range of semantic structures for first-order structures, encompassing those investigated in this work and beyond. I demonstrate how to incorporate the fundamental semantic constructs—structure, structure map, and functional relation—as well as first-order logic and its standard extensions, into this new framework. By utilizing limit and colimit properties, I derive key observations about morphisms between structures, including criteria for isomorphism, the existence of term algebras, and the behavior of interpretations. Additionally, I investigate functorial relationships between different frameworks for first-order semantics presented here.

However, the complex internal architecture of NNs often hinders their interpretability and ability to generalize. This study addresses these challenges by developing a new NnNet over-determined strategy that effectively utilizes a residual self-adaptive learning mechanism and exponential cardinality cardinalization (ECC) encoding to solve partial differential equations (PDEs). However, data is often imperfect and subject to random fluctuations, while parameters may be uncertain, varying randomly across time or spatial locations. This paper addresses the challenge of simultaneously estimating multiple parameters under such data noise and uncertainty. We introduce a Monte-Carlo based optimization algorithm that combines gradient descent with the bootstrap method to achieve this joint parameter and structure function estimation. The proposed method is demonstrated using a specific simulator for image in-water detection, illustrating how the bootstrap method is applied to estimate the random parameter $\xi$. The study includes 1,000 simulation trials to evaluate performance, reporting results as means with standard errors derived from sample variances. Numerical experiments show that the method can successfully estimate the random parameter $\xi$ and the structure function $f$, provided that a sufficient number of simulator outputs are available. For the specific detector simulator under consideration, the approach can estimate parameters and functions for frequencies up to 1,000,000 (approximately 1 meter), though accuracy diminishes at higher frequencies. Additionally, the algorithm's efficiency is confirmed, as increasing the number of bootstrap trials $B$ does not significantly degrade computational efficiency. GLAP equations for both single and double parton distribution functions (PDFs and DPDs), utilizing Chebyshev interpolation. Regarding PDF evolution, our technique achieves superior numerical accuracy with significantly fewer grid points than alternative methods. For DPD evolution, the method employs a computationally affordable number of grid points while supporting independent renormalization scales for the respective partons. Furthermore, the approach allows for fast evaluation of individual PDF or DPD slices at any desired resolution by omitting certain moments from the Chebyshev expansion. We validate both techniques through comprehensive tests involving analytically solvable cases and specific PDF/DPD sets. Finally, we apply this scheme to investigate the single parton impact factor required for hadron-level cross-section calculations at LHC energies. By providing a set of pre-computed Chebyshev coefficients, we enable the analysis of PDF/DPD and related quantities at any energy level. This eliminates the need for intensive numerical integration at $t=1$ and avoids the computational burden of solving the DPD evolution equations for every specific energy under examination. Additionally, we supply an open-source software package that implements both the numerical method and the coefficient set for the LHC's 7 and 13 TeV energies. This package is documented in a separate technical report and can be imported as a module, facilitating the solution of both PDF and DPD evolution at any energy. Complementing this, we also provide a simplified version of the method for users who do not need to compute results across multiple energies.

These samples were subjected to compression tests and X-ray Computed Tomography (CT) scanning to measure their mechanical response and internal architecture. Following the data collection, an inverse analysis was conducted to correlate the sampled microstructure with the macromechanical behavior, thereby validating the forward CT image-to-mechanical property projection. This workflow was subsequently integrated into a numerical model to predict the mechanical properties of regolith samples under varying porosity and grain size conditions. The study confirms that both porosity and grain size significantly influence the mechanical behavior of sintered regolith, a critical insight for designing experimental apparatus and structural materials and systems for Mars and the Moon. Notably, the analysis revealed a distinct difference between Lunar and Martian regolith responses: the compaction of low-porosity, fine-grained Martian regolith exhibits a unique mechanical characteristic, suggesting that the characteristic curve for compacted Martian soil may require a distinct mechanism compared to its Lunar counterpart. Case studies were provided to calculate the compaction behavior and bulk modulus of typical Lunar and Martian regolith samples and layers. These findings indicate that for the first and last meters of lunar rover compacted regolith (LRC), the bulk modulus may decrease or remain relatively stable; however, for compacted Martian regolith (MRC), the bulk modulus is expected to decline more gradually. The reported data and calculations support the design and assessment of current and future Martian and Lunar exploration equipment and systems. The study concludes that the proposed inverse analysis approach can be readily applied to various regolith types and compositions to derive a complete set of compaction models and mechanical behavior predictions. This methodology holds potential for characterizing and analyzing other granular materials and regolith simulators. Supporting this, the report includes case studies on characterizing the compaction behavior and bulk modulus of the fine-grained, high-porosity regolith simulant JSC-1A.
